entries.title: Meet Your Brain
entries.what: The brain is not one uniform organ. It is a set of specialised regions, each with a main task, that together produce perception, thought and behaviour.
entries.gives: Knowing that the mind is built from parts explains why a person can be excellent at one skill and impaired at another, and why a small injury can remove one ability while leaving the rest intact.
entries.pic: A brain seen from the side. The bronze patches are parts with their own job.

steps.t: Take a sheet of paper and a pen.
Draw the floor plan of your home from memory, every room in place.
Then draw a bicycle with its wheels, frame, seat, pedals and handlebars.
Both drawings rely on different systems: one for spatial layout, one for objects. Either can fail alone.
Watch moving water or a scrolling video for 30 seconds, then look at a still wall.
The wall appears to drift the opposite way. This is the motion aftereffect: motion-selective neurons adapt and briefly under-respond.

entries.safety: Stop if your eyes feel strained.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 1: Introduction · Lecture 2: Neuroanatomy

words.meaning: The thin, folded outer layer of the brain, about 2 to 4 mm thick, where most perception and thought take place.
The principle that distinct brain regions are dedicated to distinct tasks.
MRI images the structure of the brain; functional MRI tracks changes in blood oxygen to show which regions are active during a task.

paras: For centuries it was debated whether the brain works as a single whole or as a collection of parts. The evidence now strongly favours parts. Specific regions handle faces, places, language, music and the thoughts of other people.

This does not mean each region works alone. Regions are linked by long fibre tracts and constantly exchange information. But damage to one region often removes one function cleanly, which is the clearest proof that the functions are separate.

This part follows that idea through the whole brain: how it is built, the methods used to study it, and the specialised systems for seeing, navigating, counting, hearing, music, language and understanding others.

parts.name: Planning
parts.job: Prefrontal cortex. Plans, weighs choices, holds goals in mind and inhibits impulsive responses.

parts.name: Speaking
parts.job: Broca's area, usually on the left. Organises words into sentences and coordinates the movements of speech.

parts.name: Moving and touch
parts.job: Two parallel strips. The motor strip sends commands to the muscles; the strip behind it receives touch from the body.

parts.name: Numbers and attention
parts.job: Parietal cortex. Estimates quantity at a glance and directs attention to where it is needed.

parts.name: Seeing
parts.job: The occipital lobe. Processes everything seen, from edges and colour to motion and form.

parts.name: Hearing and music
parts.job: Auditory cortex. Turns sound into recognisable voices, words and melodies.

parts.name: Word meaning
parts.job: Language cortex in the left temporal lobe. Extracts the meaning of words and sentences.

parts.name: Other minds
parts.job: A region near the junction of the temporal and parietal lobes that represents what other people think and believe.

parts.name: Faces and places
parts.job: On the underside of the brain. One patch responds to faces, a neighbouring one to places and scenes.

parts.name: Memory and inner map
parts.job: The hippocampus. Forms new memories and maintains an internal map of the environment.

parts.name: Balance
parts.job: The cerebellum. Keeps movement smooth, timed and balanced.

parts.name: Breathing and heartbeat
parts.job: The brainstem. Runs breathing, heart rate and arousal continuously, without conscious control.

blocks.h: The man who kept getting lost
items: Bob is articulate, sociable and successful, yet he repeatedly gets lost, even on familiar routes in his own town.
After a fall, a scan finds a tumour about the size of a lime near the centre of the brain.
It sits beside a region that responds specifically to places and scenes.
He draws a bicycle accurately but cannot sketch the layout of his own home.
Surgery succeeds and he returns to work within days. His sense of direction never recovers; he relies on a phone map.
blocks.end: One region failed. Every other ability stayed intact. This is the logic of functional specialisation.

blocks.h: Six ideas that run through this part
items: The brain has parts
It is not a uniform mass. Distinct regions carry out distinct functions.
Some parts are highly specific
Separate regions for faces and for places. Damage to one leaves the other working.
Brain structure reflects the mind
Each specialised region reveals one component of how human thought is organised.
The brain changes
It develops with age and adapts with experience. Young brains recover from injury best.
The brain is the self
Hearts can be transplanted. A brain transplant would, in effect, transplant the person.
Multiple methods
Behavioural tests, scans and patient studies are combined, because each shows only part of the picture.

blocks.h: Six ways to study the living brain
items: Behavioural tests
Present a stimulus, record the response and its timing. Simple, cheap and often revealing.
Structural MRI
A detailed image of the brain's anatomy, without radiation.
Functional MRI
Shows which regions increase activity during a task, a few seconds after it happens.
Patient studies
What is lost, and what remains, after damage to a specific region.
EEG and MEG
Record electrical and magnetic signals from outside the head, with millisecond timing.
Tractography
Maps the long fibre bundles that connect regions to each other.

blocks.text: Computer vision systems can now label the objects in a photograph with high accuracy, yet still struggle to understand why a scene is funny. The human brain does both without effort.

entries.title: What Is Inside Your Head
entries.what: Beneath the skull lie a few major structures: the folded cortex, the white-matter cables beneath it, the thalamus at the centre, the hippocampus and amygdala deep in the temporal lobes, the cerebellum at the back and the brainstem below.
entries.gives: A working map of these structures makes every later topic easier to place, and explains why damage in one location produces very specific losses.
entries.pic: The brain cut down the middle, seen from the side. Front is on the left.

steps.t: Hold two pencils side by side with the tips about 5 mm apart.
Close your eyes and have someone touch your fingertip with both tips at once.
Repeat on the back of the hand, then on the forearm.
On the fingertip you feel two points; on the forearm, one. The fingertip occupies a far larger area of the touch map in the cortex.
Hum the lowest note you can, then the highest.
Low and high frequencies activate different positions along the auditory cortex, laid out in order like piano keys.

entries.safety: Press lightly, never hard enough to hurt.

words.meaning: A paired structure at the centre of the brain that relays almost all sensory input to the cortex.
A curved structure deep in the temporal lobe, essential for forming new memories and for spatial navigation.
An almond-shaped structure beside the hippocampus, central to detecting threat and processing fear.
An area of cortex where neighbouring points on the body, the visual field or the frequency scale are represented next to each other.

paras: The outer cortex is a sheet of grey matter, folded so that a surface area roughly the size of a large pizza fits inside the skull. Beneath it, nearly half the brain's volume is white matter: long fibres wrapped in fatty myelin that link one region to another.

At the centre sits the thalamus, the relay through which vision, hearing and touch pass on their way to the cortex. Smell is the exception and reaches the cortex directly. Deep in each temporal lobe lie the hippocampus, for memory and navigation, and the amygdala, for threat.

Below and behind are the cerebellum, which refines movement, and the brainstem, which controls breathing, heart rate and the sleep-wake cycle. Damage to the brainstem is far more likely to be fatal than damage to most of the cortex.

parts.name: Cortex
parts.job: The folded outer sheet where perception, language and reasoning take place. Unfolded, it covers roughly 2,500 square centimetres.

parts.name: White matter
parts.job: Bundles of myelinated fibres connecting regions to each other. Close to half of the human brain is white matter.

parts.name: Thalamus
parts.job: The central relay. Signals from the eyes, ears and skin stop here before continuing to their cortical areas.

parts.name: Hippocampus
parts.job: Forms new long-term memories and maintains an internal map of places.

parts.name: Amygdala
parts.job: Detects threat, triggers fear responses and helps recognise fear in other people's faces.

parts.name: Brainstem
parts.job: Controls breathing, body temperature, heart rate and arousal. Life depends on it.

parts.name: Cerebellum
parts.job: Refines the timing and accuracy of movement. Its folded surface resembles a cauliflower.

parts.name: Spinal cord
parts.job: The main cable to the body, carrying sensation up and motor commands down.

parts.name: Smell bulb
parts.job: Receives input from the nose. Smell is the only sense that does not pass through the thalamus first.

blocks.end: Smell is the one sense with a direct route to the cortex.

items: Visual map
Primary visual cortex holds a spatial map of the visual field. Showing people a large letter produces the same shape of activity on the cortex.
Body map
A strip across the top of the brain maps the entire body surface. Fingertips and lips have the largest areas because they are the most sensitive.
Frequency map
Auditory cortex arranges sounds from low to high pitch in an orderly line, called tonotopy.
H.M. had both hippocampi removed to treat epilepsy. Afterward he could form no new lasting memories.
An artist and pilot lost her hippocampi to a viral infection. She remains intelligent, witty and still paints, but recalls almost no events from her life.
S.M. has damage to both amygdalae. She does not experience fear and readily trusts strangers.
A boy born without a cerebellum walked late but went on to manage most everyday tasks well.
A woman who lost her motion area saw the world as a sequence of still frames, so a cup overflowed before she noticed it filling.
blocks.end: Each structure carries its own function. Lose one, and mainly that function is lost.

blocks.h: Three criteria for a true brain region
items: Distinct function
Its neurons respond to something its neighbours do not.
Distinct connections
It links to its own set of other regions, like a fingerprint.
Distinct structure
Under the microscope, its layers and cell types look different.
blocks.end: The motion area, called MT, meets all three criteria.

items: Dendrites
Branching inputs that receive signals from other neurons.
Cell body
Holds the nucleus and integrates incoming signals.
Axon
A single long fibre that carries the output signal away.
Myelin
A fatty insulating wrap that makes the signal travel many times faster.
Synapse
The narrow junction where a chemical message passes to the next cell.

blocks.text: The brain runs on about 20 watts. A well-known quiz-show computer needed around 20,000 watts to compete with human players.

entries.title: Tools to Look Inside
entries.what: Studying any mental ability starts with defining the problem the brain is solving, then testing how it is solved with behavioural experiments and brain imaging.
entries.gives: This approach explains why colour, face recognition and brain scans each reveal a different side of the same system, and why careful questions matter more than expensive machines.
entries.pic: An eye, a question mark and a scanner ring: the job, the test and the scan.

steps.t: Take a sheet of white paper.
Look at it under a warm yellow lamp, then beside a window in daylight.
It looks white both times, although the light reaching your eye differs greatly. The brain discounts the colour of the light.
Find two photos of one stranger and two photos of a well-known person.
The familiar pair matches instantly; the stranger is surprisingly hard. Face expertise applies mainly to faces we know.

Face blindness: seeing a face clearly but being unable to recognise whose it is.
The blood-oxygen change that fMRI measures. It rises a few seconds after neurons become active.

paras: A useful way to study any ability is to ask three questions in order. What problem is the brain solving, and why is it hard? What steps does the mind follow to solve it? And how do neurons carry out those steps?

Colour shows why the first question matters. The light reaching the eye mixes the colour of a surface with the colour of the light falling on it. Two unknowns, one measurement. The brain resolves this by estimating the lighting first, then inferring the surface.

Faces show the value of behavioural tests. Most people recognise familiar faces instantly from any photo, yet struggle to match two different photos of a stranger. Brain imaging then shows where in the brain this expertise lives.

items: The problem
What goes in, what must come out, and what makes the task difficult. This comes before any experiment.
The method
The sequence of steps the mind follows. Well-designed behavioural tests reveal them.
The mechanism
How neurons and circuits physically carry out those steps.
blocks.end: Studying feathers alone never explains flight. You also need aerodynamics.

items: Four photos show the same car under coloured light: teal, purple, blue and yellow.
Viewers confidently name four different car colours: red, green, yellow and blue.
Mask everything except the car body, and all four patches are the same grey.
The light reaching the eye combines surface colour and illumination colour.
The brain estimates the illumination from the scene, then subtracts it to recover the surface.
blocks.end: Colour is the brain's inference about surfaces, and it is usually correct.

blocks.text: Primates with three types of colour receptor find ripe fruit against foliage faster than those with two. Colour vision likely evolved for exactly this task.

entries.title: More Tools
entries.what: Each research method answers a different question: when the brain responds, where it responds, and whether a region is actually necessary for a task.
entries.gives: Knowing what each method can and cannot show makes it possible to judge whether a brain finding is strong or overstated.
entries.pic: A clock, a pin and a lightning bolt: timing, place, and testing a part by switching it on.

steps.t: Find a photo of a face you know well.
Turn it upside down and study it for ten seconds.
Turn it the right way up.
Inverted, it looked broadly normal. Upright, any distortion stands out. Face processing is tuned to upright faces.
Repeat with a photo of a house.
The house is affected far less by inversion. Faces are processed as a whole configuration; most objects are not.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 5: Cognitive Neuroscience Methods II

words.meaning: Electroencephalography: electrodes on the scalp record the brain's electrical activity with millisecond timing.
Two patients with opposite deficits. Together they show that two abilities depend on separate systems.
Electrodes placed directly on or in the brain, usually during epilepsy surgery.

paras: No single method answers every question. fMRI shows where activity occurs, but the blood signal lags several seconds behind. EEG and MEG capture timing to the millisecond, but locating the source is difficult.

Recordings made directly from the brain during epilepsy surgery offer both exact location and timing. They are rare and depend on patients who agree to take part while electrodes are already in place for medical reasons.
Only damage or stimulation can show that a region is necessary. A scan shows correlation: a region becomes active. Disrupting that region and observing what fails shows causation.

items: Behavioural tests
Inexpensive and often ingenious, but they show only the output, not the process.
fMRI
Good spatial detail, but slow: the signal trails neural activity by seconds.
EEG
Millisecond timing, but the signal is blurred by skull and scalp.
MEG
Similar timing to EEG, with somewhat better localisation.
Intracranial electrodes
Exact in place and time. Available only during clinical procedures.
Lesions and stimulation
The only methods that test whether a region is truly required.
blocks.end: EEG is like a microphone on a stadium roof: it picks up the crowd's roar, not individual conversations.

170 ms

130 ms

A stroke damages one man's face area. He cannot recognise faces, yet identifies objects and voices normally.
Another patient loses object recognition. He cannot tell a chair from a toaster but knows every face.
Together these opposite cases show that faces and objects rely on separate systems.
During surgery in Japan, a small current applied to the face area made the doctor's face appear to distort.
When the patient looked at a ball or a box, a face seemed to appear on top of it.
blocks.end: Stimulating the face area produces faces, and only faces.

blocks.text: One man, born face-blind, has a face area that looks normal on fMRI. Having the region is not enough; its connections to the rest of the brain matter as much.

entries.title: Testing an Idea
entries.what: A sound experiment changes one variable, measures one outcome and rules out every other explanation for the result.
entries.gives: Understanding good design lets you test claims yourself and recognise weak ones, whether in research, in the media or in your own habits.
entries.pic: Two boxes that differ in only one thing: a snake and a coiled garden hose.

steps.t: Choose a question, such as whether background music helps you remember a word list.
Write down the one variable you change (music on or off) and the one outcome you measure (words recalled).
List three other differences that could creep in: time of day, fatigue, the specific list. Hold them constant.
Run both conditions in alternating order over four days.
Compare the averages. With only one variable changed, only that variable can explain the difference.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 6: Experimental Design

words.meaning: An unintended second difference between conditions that could explain the result instead of the variable you changed.
A condition identical to the test condition except for the one factor being studied.
Transcranial magnetic stimulation: a magnetic pulse through the scalp that briefly disrupts the cortex beneath it.

paras: An experiment compares conditions that differ in exactly one respect. If the outcome differs, that one factor is the cause. The difficulty lies in making sure nothing else differs.

Suppose a region responds more to faces than to objects. Faces are also more rounded, more interesting and more familiar. Any of these could be the real cause. Each must be ruled out with a carefully chosen comparison.
Brain scans show only that a region is active. To show it is necessary, the region must be disrupted. TMS does this safely and briefly in healthy volunteers.

blocks.h: Six elements of a sound experiment
items: Independent variable
The single factor you change on purpose.
Dependent variable
The outcome you measure, such as accuracy or reaction time.
Prediction
A specific statement of what you will observe if the hypothesis is correct.
Confound
Faces are also curvier and more engaging than objects. That difference could be the true cause.
Control
Compare snakes with coiled hoses: the same shape, without the snake.
Baseline
A condition as close to "off" as possible, such as fixating a dot.

blocks.h: To prove a cause, change the cause
items: A scan shows a region becoming active. It does not prove the region is required.
TMS delivers a magnetic pulse lasting less than a millisecond over a chosen region.
Over a face-selective area near the surface, it lowers face-matching accuracy from 85 to 78 percent.
The effect appears only when the pulse arrives 60 to 100 milliseconds after the face.
In monkeys, six face patches are wired together and act as one coordinated network.
blocks.end: TMS is not used on people with a history of seizures.

blocks.text: Caffeine increases the fMRI signal. Some labs control for this by giving every volunteer the same dose before scanning.

entries.title: Faces, Places and Bodies
entries.what: Only a handful of categories have their own dedicated region in virtually every human brain: faces, places, bodies and, in readers, written words.
entries.gives: This shows which kinds of visual information the brain treats as biologically special, and raises the question of how far brain scans can read the mind.
entries.pic: The underside of a brain with three patches: a face, a house and a body.

steps.t: Find a busy photograph, such as a crowd or a street scene.
Look at it for three seconds, then close your eyes.
Describe everything you remember.
People, faces and the layout of the place come first. Each has a dedicated system.
Now name three objects from the photo.
Objects come more slowly. No single region handles cars or chairs; they are processed more diffusely.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 7: Category Selectivity, Controversies, and MVPA

words.meaning: A region responding much more strongly to one kind of stimulus, such as faces, than to others.
Multivoxel pattern analysis: reading which stimulus a person saw from the pattern of activity across many voxels.
A region on the underside of the temporal lobe that responds most strongly to faces.

paras: Scanning studies have tested many categories of image to find which ones have their own dedicated region. The list is short. Faces, places, bodies and written words each have one in almost everyone.

Many other categories that matter for survival, such as snakes, spiders, food and tools, show no such dedicated area. They are processed by more general systems spread across the ventral visual cortex.

Pattern analysis adds a further layer. Even regions with weak responses can carry information in their pattern of activity. Whether that information is actually used by the brain is a separate question.

items: Faces
A dedicated region in virtually everyone.
Places and scenes
A dedicated region in virtually everyone.
Bodies
A dedicated region in virtually everyone.
Written words
A dedicated region, but only after learning to read.
Snakes and spiders
No dedicated region found.
Food, flowers, cars, chairs
No dedicated region found.

blocks.h: Does the face area also know about chairs?
items: The challenge
Even a weak response can carry a pattern that distinguishes chairs from cars.
The finding
Pattern analysis shows that it does, to a small degree.
The reply
A vending machine can be used to tell the time from its display. That is not its function.

blocks.h: Can a scan read your mind?
items: Scan a person viewing shoes, then cats, and store each activity pattern.
Show a new image and ask which stored pattern it resembles more.
Accuracy is above chance, but modest.
It is easily defeated: small head or tongue movements, or mental arithmetic, disrupt it.
In a monkey, 167 individual neurons distinguished five faces. An fMRI scan of the same region could not.
blocks.end: Each fMRI voxel averages the activity of hundreds of thousands of neurons.

blocks.text: When people attend to letters flashing over a face, rather than the face itself, the face area responds less. Attention changes how strongly the brain processes what the eyes receive.

entries.title: Finding Your Way
entries.what: Navigation requires answering two questions continuously: where am I, and how do I reach my goal from here?
entries.gives: This identifies the brain systems that keep us oriented, and explains why some people are excellent navigators while others get lost easily.
entries.pic: A map pin, a compass arrow and a path bending around a wall.

steps.t: Stand still in a room you know well.
Close your eyes and point to the door, the window and the far wall.
Estimate the distance to each.
Open your eyes and check. You carry a spatial model of the room with you.
Walk an unfamiliar route once, then sketch it from memory.
Note which turns and landmarks you retained. These are the anchors of your mental map.

entries.safety: Stand still with your eyes closed; never walk with your eyes shut.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 8: Navigation I

words.meaning: An internal representation of the layout of an environment, allowing new routes to be planned.
Tracking position by adding up one's own movements and turns, without landmarks.
A region that responds to the spatial layout of scenes, not to the objects in them.

blocks.h: Where am I, and how do I get there?
paras: Many animals navigate across extraordinary distances with small brains. Humans rely on a combination of landmarks, the geometry of the space around them and an internal sense of direction.

A region on the underside of the brain, the parahippocampal place area, responds strongly to scenes. It reacts to the shape of the space: walls, corners and open areas. An empty room activates it as much as a furnished one.
Other regions track which way we face and how far we have moved. Together they build a cognitive map, which lets us find shortcuts we have never taken.

items: A monarch butterfly, weighing half a gram, flies more than 3,000 km to a few hectares of forest in Mexico.
The round trip spans four generations. Descendants return to the same trees their ancestors left.
Loggerhead turtles return, after up to 20 years, to the beach where they hatched.
Bats maintain their sense of direction while flying upside down in complete darkness.
A desert ant forages far from its nest, then runs straight home. Displaced, it runs the same vector from the new spot.
blocks.end: The ant tracks its own steps and turns, using no landmarks at all.

items: Recognition
Identifying a familiar place, or at least what kind of place it is.
Spatial layout
The geometry of the surroundings: walls, exits and their distances.
Heading
Which direction one faces. Leaving a subway station, you may know the corner but not the compass direction.
A cognitive map
Rats trained on a winding route take a new direct path as soon as it opens.
Reorientation
A way to reset after becoming lost.
Navigable paths
Where movement is actually possible. Glass can be seen through but not walked through.
Furnished room
Strong response.
Empty room
Equally strong.
Furniture without walls
About half the response.
Map seen from above
Weak response.
Scrambled room photo
Weak response.
Room built from LEGO
Strong response.
blocks.end: It represents the shape of space, not the objects within it.

blocks.text: When surgeons applied a small current to one patient's place area, he reported seeing a train station, a staircase and a closet full of blue objects.

entries.title: Your Inner Map
entries.what: Specialised neurons in and around the hippocampus encode where you are, which way you face and how far you have travelled.
entries.gives: These cells show how the brain maintains a live map of space, why that map sometimes flips, and how the same machinery may organise abstract thought.
entries.pic: A grid of dots in hexagons, a compass needle and one bronze spot: grid, direction and place cells.

steps.t: Sit in a swivel chair with your eyes closed while someone turns you slowly, then stops.
Point to the door.
Your internal compass still has an estimate, updated by the vestibular system in your inner ear.
With eyes open, walk ten steps, turn left and walk five more.
Without looking, point back to your starting position.
Direction and distance signals have integrated your path, much like the desert ant.

entries.safety: Stop if you feel dizzy; keep a friend beside you while your eyes are closed.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 9: Navigation II

words.meaning: A hippocampal neuron that fires when the animal occupies one specific location.
A neuron in entorhinal cortex that fires at many locations arranged in a hexagonal pattern, providing a metric for distance.
A neuron that fires when the head points in one particular direction, acting as an internal compass.

paras: In the 1970s, recordings from the rat hippocampus revealed place cells: neurons that fire only when the animal is in one particular spot. Each cell has its own spot, and together they tile the whole environment.

Later work found head-direction cells, which act as a compass, and grid cells, which fire in a hexagonal lattice across the floor and measure distance. Border cells mark walls and edges. The discoverers of place and grid cells shared the Nobel Prize in 2014.

This system is not limited to physical space. Similar grid-like patterns appear when people learn abstract relationships, suggesting that the brain uses spatial machinery to organise many kinds of information.

items: Place cells
Each fires in one location, regardless of which way the animal faces.
Head-direction cells
Each fires when the head points one way. Together they form a compass.
Grid cells
Fire at the vertices of a hexagonal grid across the environment, providing a measure of distance.
blocks.end: Border cells add walls and drop-offs. The 2014 Nobel Prize recognised place and grid cells.

items: A rat sees food hidden in one corner of a rectangular room, then is disoriented.
It searches the correct corner and the diagonally opposite one equally often. Both have the same geometry.
One distinctly coloured wall would resolve the ambiguity. The rat ignores it.
Toddlers make the same error, even when one wall is bright red and plays music.
Adults do too, when their verbal system is occupied by repeating speech aloud.
blocks.end: Colours change with the seasons; the shape of the landscape does not.

items: Abstract dimensions
Learning imaginary birds that vary in neck and leg length produces a grid-like signal.
Social space
Status and closeness can be represented like coordinates. Bats track the position of other bats.
Planning
At a junction, a rat's place cells briefly replay both possible paths before it chooses.

blocks.text: The sudden sense of facing the wrong way in a familiar place has a neural basis: the whole population of place cells can remap at once.

entries.title: Born or Learned?
entries.what: Some face-processing abilities are present within hours of birth. Experience then refines them and narrows them to the faces we actually encounter.
entries.gives: This shows nature and nurture working together rather than in opposition, and explains why early experience has such lasting effects.
entries.pic: A baby's face turning to follow a simple face drawing on a paddle.

steps.t: Find photos of two monkeys and two human strangers.
Show someone one monkey face, then both, and ask which they saw first.
Repeat with the two human faces.
Humans are easy; monkeys are hard. At six months of age, the same person could tell monkey faces apart as well.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 10: Development, Nature and Nurture I

words.meaning: A decline in looking or response to a repeated stimulus. Renewed interest in a new stimulus shows it is perceived as different.
The loss, during the first year, of the ability to discriminate stimuli that are not part of everyday experience.
Present from birth, without needing to be learned.

paras: Within an hour of birth, infants track a simple face-like pattern further than a scrambled version. Within days they can tell two unfamiliar faces apart. Some sensitivity to faces appears to be built in.

Early abilities are also broad. At six months, infants distinguish monkey faces nearly as well as human ones, and hear speech sounds from every language. By nine to twelve months, both abilities narrow to the faces and sounds they meet daily.

This narrowing is not damage. It is efficient specialisation. The same process explains why people often find faces from unfamiliar groups harder to tell apart, an effect that is largely reversible with exposure in childhood.

Show an infant the same image repeatedly.
Looking time falls with each repetition as interest fades.
Then present a new image.
If looking time rises again, the infant perceives the new image as different.
This lets researchers ask what infants can distinguish before they can speak.
blocks.end: Infants cannot answer questions, but their eyes can.

items: Faces of other species
Distinguishable at six months, largely lost by nine.
Foreign speech sounds
Infants hear contrasts from every language. Adults hear mainly those of their own.
Preserving the ability
Labelling individual monkey faces by name between 6 and 12 months maintains the skill. General exposure does not.
blocks.end: The same applies to faces of other ethnic groups. Moving to a new country before about age 12 typically reverses it.

blocks.text: Monkeys raised by caretakers wearing masks never saw a face during infancy. When they first did, they still preferred faces and could tell them apart.

entries.title: How Brains Grow
entries.what: What a brain region becomes depends heavily on the input it receives and how it is connected to the rest of the brain.
entries.gives: This explains what experience can reshape, what stays fixed, and why recovery from brain injury depends so much on age.
entries.pic: Fibres running into a patch of brain, one bronze lead ending at the reading spot.

steps.t: Choose a script you cannot read, such as Hebrew, Chinese or Arabic.
Study one line for ten seconds, then copy it from memory.
Do the same with a line in English.
English is reproduced as whole units; the unfamiliar script comes out in fragments. Your reading region is tuned to your own writing system, learned only after school began.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 11: Development, Nature and Nurture II

words.meaning: An MRI method that traces fibre bundles by following the direction in which water moves along them.
A region on the left underside of the brain that becomes specialised for written words as a person learns to read.
An early window when a brain system is especially responsive to experience.

paras: A brain region is not destined for one role from the start. Its function depends on what information reaches it and where its outputs go. Change the input early enough, and the region can take on a very different job.

Reading proves this in humans. Writing was invented only a few thousand years ago, far too recently for evolution to build a dedicated region. Yet every literate adult develops one, in nearly the same location, as they learn to read.
Flexibility declines with age. Damage early in life is often followed by remarkable recovery, as other regions take over. Similar damage in adulthood usually leaves lasting deficits.

items: Ferrets are born at an early stage, with their eyes still closed.
At birth, input from the eyes was surgically redirected to the auditory cortex.
The auditory cortex developed a layout of orientation-tuned columns typical of visual cortex.
Trained to press one lever for light and another for sound, the animals pressed the light lever when their rewired cortex was stimulated.
They experienced the input as vision.
blocks.end: The input a region receives shapes what it becomes.

items: Too recent to be innate
Writing is only a few thousand years old, too new for a genetically built region.
Acquired at school
In the same children, it is absent at age 5 and present by age 8.
Script-specific
It responds to Hebrew only in people who read Hebrew.
blocks.end: Its future location can be predicted from a child's connectivity at age 5, before reading begins.

blocks.h: What recovers and what does not
items: Adult stroke
Language rarely returns fully after damage to the left-hemisphere language areas.
Damage in infancy
Language often shifts to the right hemisphere and develops well.
Stroke at birth
One boy developed normal object recognition but never learned to recognise faces.
Congenital blindness
Visual cortex takes on roles in language and other non-visual tasks.
Blind from birth
Face-related sounds, such as laughter and chewing, still activate the usual face region.
Brain-training apps
Performance improves on the trained game, but rarely transfers to general ability.

blocks.text: Because nerve fibres are wrapped in fat, water moves along them more easily than across them. Diffusion MRI follows this water to reconstruct the brain's wiring.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.what: Humans sense approximate quantity at a glance, without counting. Infants and many animals share this ability.
entries.gives: This number sense is the foundation for later mathematics, and its strength in early childhood predicts arithmetic skill years later.
entries.pic: Two clouds of dots: the bronze cloud has twice as many.

steps.t: Take two handfuls of dried beans or coins.
Spill them into two piles. Without counting, judge which is larger.
Repeat with piles that are closer in size.
Easy when one is double the other, hard when they are close. Number sense depends on ratio, not absolute difference.
Count both piles to check your estimate.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 13: Number

words.meaning: The innate ability to estimate quantity without counting.
The ease of telling two quantities apart depends on their ratio, not their difference.
A specific, lifelong difficulty with numbers, unrelated to general intelligence.

paras: Glance at two groups of dots and you can tell which is larger without counting. The judgement is fast and approximate, and it follows a simple rule: the larger the ratio between the groups, the easier the choice.
This ability appears in newborns and across many species, from fish to bees. It works across the senses: matching a number of sounds to a number of dots is nearly as easy as comparing dots with dots.
Exact counting and arithmetic are cultural inventions built on top of this ancient system. Neurons in parietal cortex respond to specific quantities, providing a biological basis for number.

almost impossible without counting
4 days
old: infants match 12 sounds to 12 shapes
1 million
neurons in a bee brain that can add and subtract one
the age at which number sense is sharpest
4 years
how far ahead early estimation skill predicts arithmetic
Fish join the larger of two schools, which lowers their individual risk.
Lions assess how many rivals are calling before deciding whether to approach.
Male túngara frogs answer a rival's call by adding one extra note.
Rats trained on two or four flashes, given two flashes plus two tones, choose the "four" lever.
Bees learn that blue means add one and yellow means subtract one.
blocks.end: Bees even treat an empty card as less than one.

items: Ratio-based
The same rule governs judgements of brightness, weight and loudness.
Cross-modal
Comparing dots with tones is nearly as accurate as comparing dots with dots.
A mental number line
Asked whether 63 is larger than 65, people slow down as numbers get closer.
blocks.end: In parietal cortex, individual neurons are tuned to preferred quantities such as two or six.

blocks.text: A child's speed at estimating dots in kindergarten predicts arithmetic ability four years later, but not reading or general problem-solving.

entries.title: Hearing Speech
entries.what: From pressure waves in the air, the brain determines where a sound comes from, what produced it, what is being said and who is saying it.
entries.gives: This traces the steps from the ear to understanding a voice, and shows why speech recognition remains difficult even for advanced computers.
entries.pic: Sound waves entering an ear and curling into the snail-shaped cochlea.

steps.t: Sit with your eyes closed while someone moves around the room, speaking.
Point to the voice each time it changes position.
You locate it accurately without sight, using tiny differences in timing and loudness between your ears.
Ask them to drop a spoon, a pencil and a plastic cup on a table.
You identify the material of each object from sound alone.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 15: Hearing and Speech

words.meaning: The spiral structure of the inner ear that separates sound by frequency.
A visual display of sound, with frequency on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal.
The smallest unit of sound that changes meaning, such as the difference between "bat" and "pat".

paras: Hearing begins with pressure waves striking the eardrum. Three small bones transmit the vibration to the cochlea, where hair cells sort it by frequency. The signal then passes through several relay stations in the brainstem before reaching the cortex.

Auditory cortex contains a map of frequency. Next to it lie regions that respond selectively to speech and, separately, to music. The speech regions respond to the sounds of language, even in a language the listener does not understand.
Speech is hard to decode because the same word sounds different from every speaker, sounds overlap in noisy rooms, and echoes smear the signal. The brain solves all three problems in real time.

items: The scene
The kind of space and what is happening in it.
Location
Where the source is, even with eyes closed.
The source
A door, a dog, a kettle.
The material
Wood, plastic or metal.
The words
What is being said.
The speaker
Who is speaking: familiar or not, young or old.

blocks.end: Vision has one relay on its way to the cortex. Hearing has several.

items: Speaker variation
Every voice produces a different acoustic pattern for the same word.
Overlapping sources
Speech and music arrive mixed into one signal. Separating them is like solving x + y = 9 for both values.
Reverberation
Echoes blur the sound, yet also reveal the size of the room.
blocks.end: "Bat" and "pat" differ by a delay of only about 65 milliseconds before the voice begins.

blocks.text: Speech-selective regions respond just as strongly to a language the listener does not understand. They process the sounds of speech, not its meaning.

entries.title: Music
entries.what: Music appears in every known human culture and is processed by dedicated neural populations, separate from those for language.
entries.gives: This places music among core human capacities rather than as a cultural luxury, and raises the question of why it evolved.
entries.pic: A bone flute, a beat line and two notes: melody and rhythm.

steps.t: Choose a well-known song.
Hum it starting on a low note, then on a high note.
It remains the same song. You recognise the intervals between notes, not the absolute pitches. This relative pitch is rare in other species.
Clap a steady beat with another person, then have one of you skip a clap.
Both notice the gap immediately. Even sleeping newborns show a brain response to a missing beat.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 16: Music

words.meaning: Recognising a melody by the intervals between its notes, regardless of starting pitch.
A deficit in perceiving melody, present from birth or acquired after brain damage.
The perception of note combinations as smooth or pleasant. Preference for it is largely learned.

paras: Music is ancient and universal. Bone flutes date back at least 40,000 years, and surveys of hundreds of cultures find that nearly all use a small set of pitches and a regular beat.

In the brain, music and language are largely separate. Regions that respond to sentences show little response to melody, and music-selective regions show little response to speech. The music response is present even in people with no musical training.
Why music evolved is still debated. It may have served courtship, infant care or social bonding, or it may be a by-product of abilities that evolved for other purposes.

cultures surveyed: nearly all use set pitches and a beat

200 ms
for a newborn's brain to register a missing beat
8 months
later, an infant still recognises a learned melody

age at which unfamiliar rhythms stop feeling natural
Courtship
Darwin proposed that early humans sang to attract mates before language developed.
Infant care
Song reassures an infant that a caregiver is near, even when their hands are busy.
By-product
Music may exploit abilities evolved for other purposes, a view summed up as "auditory cheesecake".
Language regions show little response to music; music regions show little response to sentences.
Scanning people listening to 165 everyday sounds revealed separate speech and music components.
The music component is present even in people with no musical training.
Some neural populations respond only to song.
In a remote Bolivian community, people show no preference for consonant over dissonant chords. That preference is learned.
blocks.end: People with congenital amusia also struggle to hear whether a spoken sentence is a question.

blocks.text: At five months, infants recognise a melody they have learned, even when it is sung higher or lower than before.

entries.title: Language
entries.what: Language transfers a thought from one mind to another. Brain evidence shows it is distinct from thought itself.
entries.gives: This clarifies what language contributes to thinking, and what the mind can do without it.
entries.pic: Two heads joined by a line of sound waves, with the same bronze idea in each.

steps.t: Say "the shark bites the man", then "the man bites the shark".
Same words, opposite meaning. Word order carries it.
Close your eyes and point south. Then check.
Speakers of some Aboriginal Australian languages always know, because their language requires compass directions in everyday speech.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 18: Language I

words.meaning: The rules governing how words combine into sentences.
Loss or impairment of language after brain damage, usually to the left hemisphere.
The intended meaning of an utterance, beyond its literal words.

paras: Language has several layers: sounds or signs, words and their meanings, grammar that combines them, and the speaker's intent. A network of regions, mainly in the left frontal and temporal lobes, handles them.
This network is highly selective. It responds to sentences but not to arithmetic, logic or music. People who lose almost all language after a stroke can still reason, calculate and solve puzzles.
Language is therefore a system for communicating thought, not the medium of thought itself. It does, however, play a major role in how children learn from others.

items: Sounds and words
Speech sounds, or hand shapes in sign languages, and the concepts each word refers to.
Grammar
Rules that assign roles: "the shark bites the man" is not "the man bites the shark".
Intent
"It would be great if you could pass the salt" is a request, not an observation.
Infants of three to six months show rich reasoning before acquiring any words.
The Pirahã of the Amazon have no exact number words, yet match quantities by sight.
In 1861, a patient who could say only one syllable still showed clear understanding and thought.
People who lose nearly all language after stroke still solve arithmetic, logic problems and puzzles, and enjoy music.
An art critic losing language to a tumour wrote that his thinking remained broad and intact.
blocks.end: Language is not thought. Children, however, rely on it to learn from others.

blocks.h: A dog with a large vocabulary
items: 1,000 names
A Border Collie learned a distinct name for each of her toys.
Inference
Asked for an unfamiliar name, she chose the one toy she had not seen before.
No grammar
She could not follow sentences that specify who did what to whom.
blocks.end: Humans combine words to express ideas that have never been expressed before.

blocks.text: In some Aboriginal Australian languages, a greeting asks which direction you are heading, and an insect is described as being on your south-east leg.

entries.title: Other Minds
entries.what: Humans infer what others see, want and believe. One region, near the junction of the right temporal and parietal lobes, responds specifically to thoughts about beliefs.
entries.gives: This explains how we understand and predict one another, why the ability takes years to mature, and how it shapes moral judgement.
entries.pic: Two figures: one looks at a box, the other holds a bronze thought bubble with the box inside.

steps.t: Take two cups, a coin and a small figure.
While the figure "watches", hide the coin under cup A.
Move the figure out of view, then move the coin to cup B.
Ask a child aged 3 to 7 where the figure will look.
Most five-year-olds say A, because the figure did not see the move. Most three-year-olds say B.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 20: Mentalizing and Theory of Mind

words.meaning: The ability to attribute thoughts, beliefs and intentions to others.
A belief held by someone that no longer matches reality.
The right temporo-parietal junction, a region that responds selectively when we think about other people's thoughts.

paras: Understanding behaviour depends on inferring hidden mental states. Romeo reaches for the poison because he believes Juliet is dead. Without his belief, the action makes no sense.

Children pass simple false-belief tests around age four or five, and continue to refine the skill for years. Very young children already infer goals and offer help, but understanding that others can hold mistaken beliefs comes later.

In adults, the right temporo-parietal junction responds strongly when people consider another person's beliefs, but not their appearance, hunger or pain. Disrupting it changes how people judge accidental harm.

items: One pirate places his sandwich on a chest and leaves for a drink.
The wind blows it onto the grass. A second pirate places his own sandwich on the chest.
A five-year-old predicts the first pirate will think the remaining sandwich is his.
A three-year-old predicts he will take his own, explaining that it was dirty.
Only around age seven do children say the blame belongs to the wind.
blocks.end: Understanding that others can hold false beliefs takes years to develop fully.

items: Perception
What another person has seen, and what they have missed.
Desire
What they want. Romeo reaches for the poison because he wants to die.
Belief
What they hold to be true. He believes Juliet is dead; she is not.
Another person's thoughts
Strong response.
Their appearance
Little response.
Their hunger or pain
Little response.
A silent animated film
Strong at moments when characters form beliefs.
Development
Becomes more selective through childhood after age four.
Disrupted with TMS
Accidental harm is judged more harshly.
blocks.end: Whether a person believed a powder was sugar or poison changes how we judge the same outcome.

blocks.text: At 18 months, toddlers spontaneously help an adult whose hands are full, without being asked or rewarded.

entries.title: Brain Teams
entries.what: Brain regions work in networks connected by long fibre tracts. These networks remain coordinated even at rest.
entries.gives: This shows how regions combine their work, and identifies the network that supports general problem-solving and fluid intelligence.
entries.pic: Three bronze dots linked by curved fibres, and two grey dots linked to each other.

steps.t: Lie down for five minutes with your eyes closed and no task.
Notice where your thoughts go.
Memories, plans and other people. This is the default network at work.
Then calculate 17 × 13 in your head.
Notice the shift. The multiple-demand network takes over for effortful tasks.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 21: Brain Networks

words.meaning: Long nerve fibres wrapped in myelin, connecting distant brain regions.
Regions most active during rest, mind-wandering and thinking about oneself or others.
Frontal and parietal regions that activate for any difficult cognitive task.

paras: Specialised regions do not work alone. Long fibre tracts link them into networks, and regions within a network rise and fall in activity together, even when a person is simply resting in a scanner.
Three networks are especially clear. The default mode network is active during mind-wandering. The multiple-demand network engages for any hard task. The language network stays distinct from both.
The multiple-demand network appears to be the brain's general-purpose problem solver. Damage to it lowers fluid intelligence in proportion to the tissue lost, while similar damage elsewhere does not.

items: of the human brain is white matter (about 10% in mice)
3x

Default mode
Active when no external task is given: memory, planning and social thought.
Multiple demand
Engages for any difficult task: working memory, arithmetic, fine discrimination.
Language
Its regions fluctuate together even 10 to 12 cm apart, and separately from the multiple-demand network.
The inputs a region receives determine what information it can represent.
Its outputs determine what it can influence.
Children with dyslexia show a less organised tract between two language regions.
Brains minimise wiring length, like a well-designed circuit board, because fibres cost space and metabolic fuel.
Damage to the multiple-demand network lowers IQ in proportion to tissue lost. Damage elsewhere does not.
blocks.end: The multiple-demand network is the brain's general-purpose problem solver.

blocks.text: Resting-state scans require no task at all. Volunteers often fall asleep while the scanner maps their networks.

entries.title: Attention and Awareness
entries.what: Attention selects a small fraction of sensory input for awareness and filters out the rest.
entries.gives: This reveals how much of the visual world goes unnoticed, and how deliberate attention shapes what we experience.
entries.pic: An eye with a bronze beam lighting one shape among many grey ones.

steps.t: Find a pair of "spot the difference" images.
Alternate between them once per second without searching.
Many changes remain invisible. This is change blindness.
Now examine one small region at a time.
The differences appear. Awareness follows attention.
Fix your eyes on someone's nose while they hold fingers out to the side. Count them without moving your eyes.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.13 The Human Brain · Prof. Nancy Kanwisher · Lecture 24: Attention and Awareness

words.meaning: Prioritising some information for processing while suppressing the rest.
Failure to notice large changes in a scene when attention is elsewhere.
When each eye sees a different image, awareness alternates between them while the input stays constant.

paras: The senses deliver far more information than the brain can fully process. Attention selects what reaches awareness. The result is that people often miss large, obvious changes when their attention is directed elsewhere.
Attention can move with the eyes, which jump two to four times per second, or independently of them. Even while fixating one point, it is possible to attend to an object in peripheral vision.

In the brain, attention increases responses in the regions processing the attended item. Frontal and parietal regions control where attention goes. Damage to them can leave a person able to see only one object at a time.

items: A street scene flashes repeatedly while awnings, colours and a car change. Most viewers miss most changes.
In a short film, the set changes between every shot. Viewers notice almost none of it.
Trained pilots in a flight simulator often landed straight through an aircraft parked on the runway.
Afterward, many refused to believe it had been there.
A hands-free phone call still divides limited attention while driving.
blocks.end: Attention is a filter: limited in capacity and directed by choice.

items: Overt attention
The eyes move two to four times per second. The central fovea occupies a disproportionately large share of visual cortex.
Covert attention
With the eyes fixed on one point, attention can still shift to an object in the periphery.
Feature selection
Attending to red letters among blue ones filters out the blue at little cost.
Amplification
The face area responds far more strongly when faces are attended.
Early filtering
Effects appear even in the thalamus, the first relay after the eye.
Control network
Frontal and parietal regions direct where attention goes.
Bilateral damage
Some patients can perceive only one object at a time.
Rivalry
A face shown to one eye and a house to the other: awareness alternates while the input stays the same.
Unseen processing
A scene that is not consciously seen still produces a small response in the place area.

blocks.text: A pike catches its first fish faster when one stickleback is in the tank than when there are ten. Too many targets split attention, even in fish.

entries.title: The Retina and the Blind Spot
entries.what: The retina is a thin sheet of neurons at the back of the eye. Rods and cones catch light, and two main kinds of ganglion cell send a compressed report to the brain.
entries.gives: The design of the retina explains sharp central vision, poor night vision in the centre, the blind spot, and why our eyes face forward.
entries.pic: A cross and a dot. At the right distance the dot (bronze) vanishes into the blind spot.

steps.t: On paper, draw a small cross on the left and a dot 8 cm to the right.
Hold the paper at arm's length. Close your left eye.
Look only at the cross with your right eye and slowly bring the paper closer.
At one distance the dot disappears and the paper looks whole. The brain filled the gap where the optic nerve leaves the eye.
Open both eyes and repeat.
The dot stays visible. The two blind spots fall on different parts of the scene, so each eye covers for the other.
At night, look slightly beside a faint star instead of straight at it.
It looks brighter off-centre. The very centre of the retina has cones only and no rods.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.04 Sensory Systems · Layout of the visual system and the retina

words.meaning: The small central pit of the retina, packed with cones and used for sharp vision.
The output cell of the retina. Its axons form the optic nerve.
The crossing point under the brain where fibres from the inner half of each retina switch sides.
The brain supplying what belongs in a gap so the picture looks whole.

paras: Light passes through several layers of neurons before it reaches the rods and cones at the back of the retina. The signal then travels forward again, through bipolar cells to ganglion cells, whose axons leave the eye together as the optic nerve.
Where those axons exit there is no room for receptors. That patch is the blind spot. You never notice it, because the brain fills it in and because the other eye sees what it misses.

Animals with eyes on the side of the head see almost all round. Primates gave up the rear view for a large overlap between the two eyes, which gives fine depth. To make that work, fibres from the inner half of each retina cross to the other side of the brain.

rods, for dim light
6 million
cones, for daylight and colour
cones per square millimetre in the fovea
1 in 8
cones is a blue cone
1 degree

Rods
Very sensitive, used at night, colour-blind. Absent from the fovea, so the centre of vision is poor in the dark.
Cones
Work in daylight, give sharp vision and colour. Packed most densely in the fovea.
Light makes them quieter
In darkness receptors release transmitter steadily. Light reduces that release.
Rods and cones catch light at the back of the retina.
Horizontal cells link neighbouring receptors and create the surround of each receptive field.
Bipolar cells carry the signal inward. Half respond to light, half to dark.
Amacrine cells, more than 20 kinds, shape timing and handle the rod signal.
Ganglion cells fire spikes and send the result to the brain through the optic nerve.
blocks.end: Receptors, horizontal and bipolar cells use graded voltages. Only the last stage fires spikes.

items: Midget cells
Small fields fed by a single cone in the centre of the retina. They signal fine detail and colour, with a sustained response.
Parasol cells
Fields about three times wider, fed by mixed cones. They signal motion and change, with a brief burst.
Centre and surround
Most cells respond to a small spot in the centre and are inhibited by light around it, so they report contrast.

blocks.text: The image on the retina is upside down. In one experiment, words shown to a mouse could be read, inverted, in the pattern of activated cells on its flattened retina.

entries.title: Welcome to Neuroscience
entries.what: Neuroscience studies the nervous system at every scale, from single molecules to conscious thought, around one central question: how does physical tissue produce a mind?
entries.gives: It sets out the map for the whole part and shows how the idea that the brain, not the heart, governs behaviour was argued over for thousands of years before it was proven.
entries.pic: A brain, the spinal cord below it and nerves branching out. One bronze cell stands for 100 billion.

steps.t: Sit upright, close your eyes and rest both hands on your knees.
Bring one index finger to the tip of your nose without looking.
Stretch receptors in your muscles and joints reported the arm's position. This sense is called proprioception.
Name three separate sounds in the room.
Each sound passed from the ear through the brainstem and thalamus to the cortex in well under a second.
Place one hand on your forehead and the other on the back of your head.
Behind the forehead sits planning and judgement; at the back sits vision. Function follows location.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 1: Neuroscience: Past, Present and Future

words.meaning: A nerve cell: the cell type that receives, combines and sends electrical signals.
The principle that different regions of the brain handle different tasks.
The scales at which the brain is studied: molecular, cellular, systems, behavioural and cognitive.

paras: Neuroscience is a young name for an old question. The Society for Neuroscience was founded in 1970, but people have argued about where thought lives for at least seven thousand years. Today the field joins biology, chemistry, physics, medicine and psychology.

The work moves across scales. A single ion channel opening in a membrane, a circuit in the spinal cord and a decision made in the frontal lobe are all part of one system. Each level explains the one above it and is limited by the one below.

This part follows the same order as the course: first the single cell, then the major systems for sensing and moving, and finally behaviour, including memory, attention, emotion, sleep and mental illness.

items: The cell
Topics 2 to 6 cover how one neuron holds an electrical charge, fires a signal and passes it to the next cell through chemistry.
The systems
Topics 7 to 14 cover the layout of the brain, then vision, hearing, smell, taste and the control of movement.
Behaviour
Topics 15 to 22 cover brain chemistry, mental illness, motivation, memory, attention, emotion and sleep.
blocks.end: Each level rests on the one before it, so the order matters.

items: Prehistoric skulls show deliberate holes drilled in living people. Healed bone proves many survived the procedure.
Ancient Egyptian physicians placed the mind in the heart. The brain was removed through the nose before burial and discarded.
Hippocrates argued that the brain is the organ of feeling and thought. Aristotle disagreed and saw it as a radiator that cools the blood.
Galen, physician to Roman gladiators, studied sheep brains and described fluid-filled ventricles. His model held for 1,500 years.
Renaissance anatomists turned to the tissue itself and separated grey matter, rich in cells, from white matter, made of fibres.
blocks.end: The correct view existed early. It took evidence, not authority, to make it stick.

blocks.h: Six findings that built the modern field
items: Nerves are wires
Electrical stimulation makes muscles twitch, and the brain itself produces electrical current. Nerves conduct signals, not fluid.
One-way traffic
In each spinal nerve, the rear root carries sensation in and the front root carries commands out to the muscles.
Bumps mean nothing
Phrenology claimed character could be read from skull shape. It was popular, untested and wrong.
Place predicts function
A patient who lost speech but kept comprehension had damage in one area of the left frontal lobe, now called Broca's area.
Shared ancestry
Darwin noted that fear and anger look alike across mammals. This is why animal research applies to human brains.
The neuron
By 1900, staining methods showed the nervous system is built from separate cells, each a discrete unit.
Molecular
The proteins, transmitters and genes that build neurons and carry their messages.
Cellular
How a single neuron receives input, makes a decision and sends output to other cells.
Systems
Circuits of neurons that work together for one purpose, such as seeing or walking.
Behavioural
How systems combine to produce memory, mood, language and dreaming.
Cognitive
How neural activity gives rise to self-awareness, mental imagery and abstract thought.
The method
Observe, replicate, interpret and submit to review. Independent checking is what catches error and fraud.

entries.title: Neurons and Their Helpers
entries.what: A neuron has a cell body, branching dendrites that receive input and a single axon that sends output. Glial cells surround it and supply, insulate, clean and protect.
entries.gives: Every later topic depends on these parts. The shape of a neuron also tells you a great deal about its role in a circuit.
entries.pic: One neuron: branches on the left, the cell body, and a long axon wrapped in bronze myelin.

steps.t: Hold one hand up with the fingers spread.
Read the fingers as dendrites, the palm as the cell body and the forearm as the axon.
Slide a coin from the palm to the elbow.
This models anterograde transport: proteins carried outward along microtubules at up to 1,000 mm a day.
Slide the coin back to the palm.
This models retrograde transport. Herpes and rabies viruses use the same return route to reach the cell body.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 2: Neurons and Glia

words.meaning: The single output fibre of a neuron. In the body it can exceed one metre in length.
A small protrusion on a dendrite that receives one synaptic input and changes shape with experience.
Layers of glial membrane wrapped around an axon that make conduction many times faster.

blocks.h: The cell that does the thinking
paras: The brain holds roughly 100 billion neurons and at least as many glial cells. A neuron shares the basic equipment of any cell: a nucleus, mitochondria for fuel and ribosomes for building proteins. What sets it apart is shape.

Dendrites form a branching tree that collects input from thousands of other cells. The axon is a single cable, even in width, that carries the output. Where an axon ends on another cell, it forms a synapse.
Glia were long seen as packing material. They are now known to regulate the chemical environment, insulate axons, remove debris and shape how synapses form and work.

blocks.h: A century of staining and argument
items: Brain tissue is soft and colourless. Fixatives were needed to harden it and thin slices to see through it.
The Nissl stain marks cell bodies, which made the layered structure of the cortex visible for the first time.
Golgi found a silver stain that fills a small number of cells completely, showing every branch.
Cajal used Golgi's method to argue that neurons are separate cells that touch rather than fuse.
Both shared the Nobel Prize in 1906. The electron microscope later confirmed that Cajal was right.
blocks.end: Golgi held to the opposite view, a continuous network, until the end.

items: Nucleus
Holds the DNA. Genes are copied into messenger RNA, which leaves the nucleus to be read.
Rough ER
Stacks of membrane studded with ribosomes, where most proteins are made. Neurons have large amounts of it.
Mitochondria
Convert glucose and oxygen into ATP, the cell's fuel. Synapses are especially rich in them.
Axon hillock
The base of the axon, where the decision to fire is made. Its membrane carries dense ion channels.
Axon terminal
The end of the axon, packed with vesicles of transmitter ready to release onto the next cell.
Dendrites
The input tree. Their surface is covered with receptors for transmitters released by other neurons.

blocks.h: Classified by shape, length and chemistry
items: By number of branches
Unipolar, bipolar and multipolar neurons have one, two or many processes. Most brain neurons are multipolar.
By dendrite shape
Pyramidal cells in the cortex have a triangular body; stellate cells are star-shaped.
By spines
Spiny neurons tend to be excitatory. Smooth, spineless neurons are usually inhibitory.
By connection
Sensory neurons receive from the senses, motor neurons drive muscles and interneurons connect neurons to each other.
By axon length
Projection neurons send long axons to other regions; local circuit neurons stay within one area.
By transmitter
Cells that release acetylcholine are called cholinergic; those that release dopamine, dopaminergic.
Astrocytes
Fill the space between neurons, absorb excess transmitter and control the ion balance that neurons depend on.
Myelinating glia
Oligodendrocytes in the brain and Schwann cells in the body wrap axons in myelin. Gaps between wraps are the nodes of Ranvier.
Microglia
The brain's immune cells. They remove debris from dead cells and are increasingly linked to synapse pruning.
blocks.end: Ependymal cells also line the fluid-filled ventricles and help guide cell migration during development.

entries.title: The Resting Neuron
entries.what: At rest, the inside of a neuron sits about 65 millivolts more negative than the outside. That stored charge comes from uneven ion concentrations and a membrane that lets potassium leak out.
entries.gives: This resting charge is the battery that powers every signal. Without it, no neuron can fire.
entries.pic: A cell wall with potassium (bronze) crowded inside and sodium (grey) crowded outside.

steps.t: Picture a membrane with potassium inside and sodium outside.
Open only potassium channels in your mind.
Potassium flows out down its concentration gradient, leaving the inside negative.
Let the negative charge build until it pulls potassium back as hard as the gradient pushes it out.
That balance point is the equilibrium voltage for potassium, about minus 80 millivolts.
Add a small sodium leak.
The resting value settles slightly less negative, about minus 65. The sodium-potassium pump keeps the gradients in place.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 3: The Neuronal Membrane at Rest

words.meaning: An atom with an electrical charge. Sodium and potassium are positive; chloride is negative.
The charge at which an ion's electrical pull exactly balances its concentration push, so no net flow occurs.
A membrane protein that uses ATP to push sodium out and pull potassium in, three for two.

blocks.h: Why a cell holds a charge
paras: A neuron is not a copper wire. Its interior is a salty fluid with poor conductivity, and the membrane leaks. To move signals over distance, it relies on stored electrical charge across its membrane.
Two things create that charge. Pumps keep potassium concentrated inside the cell and sodium outside. Then channels that are selective for potassium let it leak out, carrying positive charge with it.
As positive charge leaves, the inside turns negative and begins to pull potassium back. The resting value is where those two forces balance, adjusted slightly by a small leak of sodium.

blocks.h: Why a neuron cannot work like a cable
items: Poor conductor
The fluid inside an axon resists current far more than metal. A passive signal fades within a few millimetres.
Leaky insulation
The membrane lets charge escape along its length, like a garden hose with holes.
The solution
A stored charge that can be released at every point along the axon, renewing the signal as it travels.
Water
The solvent. Its slightly charged molecules surround ions and keep them dissolved.
Ions
Sodium, potassium, calcium and chloride carry charge through the fluid on both sides.
Lipid bilayer
The membrane's double layer of fat blocks ions completely. Only proteins can let them through.
Ion channels
Protein pores that open for specific ions. Potassium channels pass potassium but not the smaller sodium.
Ion pumps
Proteins that spend ATP to move ions against their gradients and build up concentration differences.
Charge separation
A thin layer of charge sits on each side of the membrane. The bulk fluid stays neutral.
Diffusion
Ions move from high to low concentration, provided a channel is open for them.
Electrical force
Opposite charges attract and like charges repel, so the membrane voltage pushes or pulls on each ion.
Balance
For each ion there is one voltage where the two forces cancel. This is described by the Nernst equation.
The pump moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in for every ATP it spends.
Potassium is now about twenty times more concentrated inside than outside.
Potassium leak channels let it flow outward, carrying positive charge out of the cell.
The inside becomes negative and starts to hold potassium back.
At about minus 65 millivolts, outward push and inward pull reach a steady state.
blocks.end: The membrane at rest is about forty times more permeable to potassium than to sodium.
