blocks.h: Why the brain controls it so tightly
items: The resting charge depends most on the potassium level outside the cell.
A rise in outside potassium makes neurons less negative and easier to fire.
The blood-brain barrier keeps blood potassium swings from reaching brain tissue.
Astrocytes absorb excess potassium and spread it through their linked network.
Lethal injection uses potassium chloride because it stops the heart by collapsing this charge.
blocks.end: Small changes here have large effects on how excitable the whole brain is.

blocks.text: The first potassium channel gene was found in a fruit fly mutant that shakes its legs under anaesthesia. The gene was named Shaker, and the channel family that followed shares the name.

entries.title: The Spike
entries.what: A spike is a brief reversal of the membrane charge, about one millisecond long, that travels down the axon without fading. It is the neuron's basic unit of information.
entries.gives: Spikes are how the nervous system transmits every sensation, thought and command over distance. Their timing and rate carry the message.
entries.pic: A flat line, a sharp bronze peak, a small dip below rest, then flat again.

steps.t: Picture the axon at rest, minus 65 millivolts inside.
Push the charge up to the threshold, about minus 50.
Voltage-gated sodium channels open. Sodium rushes in and the inside turns positive within half a millisecond.
Hold for a moment.
Sodium channels inactivate and potassium channels open. Potassium leaves and the charge falls back.
Note the brief overshoot below the resting value.
During this refractory period, a new spike is hard or impossible to trigger. This keeps the signal moving in one direction.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 4: The Action Potential

words.meaning: The voltage at which enough sodium channels open to trigger a full spike.
A short window after a spike when the neuron cannot fire again, or needs a much stronger input.
The way a spike jumps from one gap in the myelin to the next, which greatly increases speed.

paras: A spike either happens fully or not at all. Once the membrane reaches threshold, the same shape and size of signal follows every time. Stronger input does not make a bigger spike; it makes more spikes per second.

The mechanism was worked out in the 1950s using the giant axon of the squid, about a millimetre wide. Later, the patch-clamp method allowed scientists to record the current through a single channel protein.
Speed depends on axon width and insulation. Thin bare axons conduct at about one metre per second. Thick myelinated axons reach over one hundred, fast enough to coordinate a whole body in real time.

items: Rising phase: sodium channels open and sodium floods in. The inside swings positive.
Overshoot: the charge peaks near plus 40 millivolts, close to the sodium equilibrium.
Falling phase: sodium channels inactivate and potassium channels open. Charge drops.
Undershoot: potassium keeps flowing briefly, taking the cell below its resting value.
Recovery: channels reset and the membrane returns to rest, ready for the next spike.
blocks.end: The whole cycle takes about two milliseconds.

items: Rate
A stronger stimulus produces a higher firing rate, up to about 1,000 spikes per second in some cells.
Timing
The exact pattern and timing of spikes can carry additional information beyond rate.
Direction
The refractory period prevents a spike from travelling backward, so signals move one way along the axon.
Hodgkin and Huxley recorded from the squid giant axon in the 1940s and 1950s.
They used a voltage clamp to hold the membrane at a set value and measure ion currents.
Their mathematical model predicted the spike shape. They won the Nobel Prize in 1963.
Neher and Sakmann developed the patch clamp to record from single channels.
Gene cloning then revealed the structure of the sodium channel protein itself.
blocks.end: The squid axon is large because it drives the animal's fast escape jet.

blocks.h: Two ways to speed a signal
items: Wider axon
A thicker axon offers less internal resistance, so current spreads farther and faster.
Myelin
Insulating wraps stop current leaking out between gaps, so the signal jumps from node to node.
Nodes of Ranvier
Short bare gaps packed with sodium channels, where the spike is renewed about every millimetre.
Tetrodotoxin
Found in puffer fish. It plugs sodium channels and can stop breathing within hours.
Saxitoxin
Made by algae in red tides and concentrated in shellfish. It also blocks sodium channels.
Batrachotoxin
From a Colombian frog. It holds sodium channels open, so neurons cannot reset.
Local anaesthetics
Lidocaine and similar drugs block sodium channels in pain fibres, stopping signals reaching the brain.
Scorpion toxins
Some slow sodium channel inactivation and extend each spike.
Medical use
Each toxin binds one site, which made them essential tools for mapping channel structure.
Multiple sclerosis
The immune system attacks myelin in the brain and spinal cord, slowing or blocking signals.
Symptoms
Weakness, numbness, visual loss and poor coordination, depending on which tracts are affected.
Peripheral loss
Guillain-Barré syndrome attacks the myelin of nerves in the body, often after an infection.

blocks.text: If the 100 billion neurons of one brain were laid out end to end with their axons, the total length would wrap the Earth several times.

entries.title: How Neurons Talk
entries.what: At a synapse, an electrical spike in one neuron triggers the release of a chemical messenger that changes the charge of the next neuron.
entries.gives: Synapses are where information is combined, filtered and stored. Most drugs that act on the brain work here.
entries.pic: Two cell ends with a narrow gap. Small bronze dots cross from the left to the right.

steps.t: Picture a spike arriving at an axon terminal.
Let the charge open calcium channels in the terminal.
Calcium enters and triggers vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release transmitter.
Follow the transmitter across a gap of about 20 to 50 nanometres.
It binds receptors on the next cell, opening channels or starting chemical cascades.
Now remove the transmitter.
It is broken down by enzymes or taken back up into cells, which ends the signal in milliseconds.

entries.safety: Breathe gently and stop if you feel dizzy.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 5: Synaptic Transmission

words.meaning: A small membrane sphere inside the axon terminal that stores transmitter molecules.
Small shifts in charge that make a neuron more likely (excitatory) or less likely (inhibitory) to fire.
The way a neuron adds up thousands of inputs across space and time to decide whether to fire.

blocks.h: Electrical in, chemical across, electrical out
paras: Most synapses are chemical. A spike reaches the end of the axon, calcium enters and vesicles release transmitter into a narrow gap. Receptors on the far side respond within a fraction of a millisecond.
A small number of synapses are electrical. Here, channels called gap junctions connect two cells directly, and current flows across with no delay. They are useful where many cells must fire together.

Each neuron receives thousands of inputs. Some push it toward firing, some hold it back. The cell adds them together at the base of the axon, and only if the total crosses threshold does it send a spike.

items: In the early 1900s, it was unclear whether synapses were electrical or chemical.
Otto Loewi woke one night in 1921 with an experiment in mind, wrote it down and could not read his notes in the morning.
The idea returned the next night. He stimulated the vagus nerve of a frog heart, which slowed it.
He moved fluid from that heart to a second heart, which slowed as well.
The nerve had released a chemical, later identified as acetylcholine. He won the Nobel Prize in 1936.
blocks.end: One clear experiment ended decades of debate.

items: Electrical
Gap junctions join two cells so current flows directly. Fast, two-way and common in early development.
Chemical
Transmitter crosses a gap and binds receptors. Slower but flexible, and able to amplify, invert or modify a signal.
Where they sit
Axon to dendrite is most common, but synapses also form on cell bodies, spines and other axon terminals.

blocks.h: Across the gap, step by step
items: Synthesis
Transmitters are made in the terminal or carried there from the cell body.
Storage
Vesicles collect transmitter and dock near release sites on the terminal membrane.
Calcium entry
The spike opens voltage-gated calcium channels. Calcium is the trigger for release.
Fusion
SNARE proteins pull the vesicle into the membrane and its contents spill into the gap.
Binding
Transmitter binds receptors on the target cell, opening channels or activating G-proteins.
Clearance
Enzymes, reuptake pumps and diffusion end the signal so the synapse can respond again.
EPSP
An excitatory input lets positive ions in, nudging the cell toward threshold.
IPSP
An inhibitory input lets chloride in or potassium out, moving the cell away from threshold.
Spatial summation
Inputs arriving at the same moment on different dendrites add together.
Temporal summation
Inputs arriving in quick succession at one synapse build on each other.
Shunting
Inhibition near the cell body can cancel excitation flowing in from distant dendrites.
Modulation
Some transmitters act slowly through chemical cascades, adjusting how a cell responds for minutes.
Thousands of synapses deliver small inputs, each worth a fraction of a millivolt.
Charge spreads along dendrites and fades with distance.
At the axon hillock, all incoming changes are summed.
If the total reaches threshold, a spike fires down the axon.
Inhibitory inputs placed close to the hillock carry the most weight.
blocks.end: Position on the cell matters as much as strength.

blocks.h: Drugs and poisons at the synapse
items: Botulinum toxin
Blocks acetylcholine release at muscles. Used in small doses to relax wrinkles and spasms.
Black widow venom
Triggers massive release of acetylcholine, causing cramps and spasms.
Curare
Blocks acetylcholine receptors on muscle. Once used on arrow tips, later in surgery.
Nerve gas
Blocks the enzyme that clears acetylcholine, so muscles cannot relax.
Agonists
Drugs that mimic a transmitter and activate its receptors.
Antagonists
Drugs that block a receptor without activating it.

blocks.text: A rare startle condition described in nineteenth-century Maine lumberjacks, the Jumping Frenchmen, involves an extreme reaction to sudden sounds. A similar disorder, hyperekplexia, is caused by faulty glycine receptors, which normally provide inhibition in the spinal cord.

entries.title: Messengers at the Gap
entries.what: Neurotransmitters are the chemical messengers released at synapses. The same transmitter can excite one cell and inhibit another, depending on the receptor it meets.
entries.gives: Understanding transmitters and their receptors explains how medicines, caffeine, alcohol and recreational drugs change thought and mood.
entries.pic: Three keys of different shapes, each fitting its own lock.

steps.t: Pick one transmitter, such as dopamine.
Ask where it is made and which cells release it.
Dopamine comes from small groups of cells in the midbrain that send axons widely.
Ask which receptors it meets.
Dopamine has at least five receptor types, all acting through G-proteins.
Ask how the signal ends.
A reuptake pump returns it to the terminal. Cocaine blocks this pump, so dopamine lingers.

entries.safety: Read only. Never change a medicine without your doctor.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 6: Neurotransmitter Systems

words.meaning: A receptor that is itself a channel. It opens within a millisecond of binding transmitter.
A receptor that acts through G-proteins and second messengers. Slower, longer lasting and able to amplify.
A small molecule inside the cell, such as cyclic AMP, that carries a receptor's signal to its targets.

paras: Amino acids such as glutamate, GABA and glycine handle most fast signalling. Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter in the brain; GABA is the main inhibitory one.

Amines, including acetylcholine, dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin and histamine, come from smaller groups of cells and often adjust the state of whole regions. Peptides, longer chains of amino acids, act more slowly and are released under heavy activity.
The receptor decides the effect. Acetylcholine excites skeletal muscle through one receptor type and slows the heart through another. One messenger, many meanings.

items: Glutamate
The main excitatory transmitter in the brain. Essential for learning, and toxic in excess.
GABA
The main inhibitory transmitter. Calming drugs such as benzodiazepines boost its effect.
Acetylcholine
Drives skeletal muscle and supports attention and memory in the brain.
Dopamine
Involved in movement, motivation and reward. Lost in Parkinson's disease.
Serotonin
Shapes mood, sleep and appetite. Target of the most common antidepressants.
Peptides
Include endorphins and substance P. They modulate pain, stress and appetite.

blocks.h: How a chemical is proven to be a transmitter
items: Location
It must be made and stored in the presynaptic neuron.
Release
It must be released when the axon terminal is stimulated.
Mimicry
Applying it directly must reproduce the effect of natural release on the target cell.
Ionotropic
A channel with a binding site. Glutamate AMPA and NMDA receptors and GABA-A receptors work this way.
Metabotropic
Activates G-proteins inside the cell, which open channels or start chemical cascades.
Amplification
One activated receptor can trigger thousands of second-messenger molecules, multiplying the signal.

blocks.h: What common substances do at the synapse
items: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors. Adenosine builds during waking and promotes sleep.
Nicotine activates one type of acetylcholine receptor, including in reward circuits.
Alcohol enhances GABA receptors and dampens glutamate receptors.
Cocaine blocks reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine, extending their action.
SSRIs block reuptake of serotonin. Their mood effects take weeks to build.
blocks.end: Each drug works by borrowing or blocking a system that already exists.

items: Morphine binds opioid receptors, which the brain already uses for its own endorphins.
Endorphins are released under stress and pain and reduce the perception of pain.
Cannabis acts on cannabinoid receptors, among the most common receptors in the brain.
The brain makes its own cannabinoids, such as anandamide, on demand.
These travel backward across the synapse and reduce transmitter release.
blocks.end: Finding a drug receptor usually means finding a natural messenger.

entries.title: The Brain's Floor Plan
entries.what: The nervous system develops from a simple tube in the embryo. Its regions, from spinal cord to cortex, follow from how that tube swells and folds.
entries.gives: A clear map of the regions and directions makes every later topic easier to place and remember.
entries.pic: A tube with three swellings: the front (bronze), the middle and the back.

steps.t: Place one hand flat on top of your head, facing forward.
Move it toward the forehead.
That is rostral, toward the nose. The back of the head is caudal.
Move it to the top of the head.
That is dorsal. The underside of the brain is ventral.
Point to the middle line between your eyes.
That is medial. Toward the ears is lateral. These terms locate any structure in the brain.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 7: The Structure of the Nervous System

words.meaning: The hollow tube in the early embryo that becomes the brain and spinal cord.
Connected chambers inside the brain filled with cerebrospinal fluid.
Three protective membranes around the brain: dura, arachnoid and pia.

paras: Three weeks after conception, a flat sheet of cells on the embryo's back rolls into a tube. Its front end swells into three chambers: forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain. The rest becomes the spinal cord.

The forebrain later divides into the cerebral hemispheres and the diencephalon, which holds the thalamus and hypothalamus. The midbrain stays small. The hindbrain forms the cerebellum, pons and medulla.

In humans the hemispheres grow so large that they fold over everything else. Folding increases surface area, and most of that surface is neocortex, the six-layered tissue that handles perception, language and planning.

items: A flat neural plate forms on the back of the embryo in the third week.
Its edges rise and fuse to form the neural tube, closing by the fourth week.
The front end swells into forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain.
The hemispheres grow outward and backward, folding as they expand.
Failure to close causes spina bifida or anencephaly. Folic acid before pregnancy lowers the risk.
blocks.end: The fluid space inside the tube becomes the ventricles.

blocks.h: Major regions of the adult brain
items: Cerebrum
The two hemispheres. Cortex on the surface, white matter and deep nuclei below.
Thalamus
The relay station that passes nearly all sensory input to the cortex.
Hypothalamus
Controls hormones, body temperature, hunger, thirst and daily rhythms.
Midbrain
Contains centres for eye movements, hearing reflexes and dopamine cells.
Cerebellum
Coordinates movement and timing. Contains more neurons than the rest of the brain combined.
Pons and medulla
Carry tracts between brain and body and control breathing and heart rate.
Rostral and caudal
Toward the nose and toward the tail. In the human brain, front and back.
Dorsal and ventral
Toward the back and toward the belly. In the brain, top and bottom.
Medial and lateral
Toward the midline and toward the side. Ipsilateral means same side, contralateral opposite.
The skull forms a rigid outer shell.
The dura mater is a tough leather-like layer just inside the skull.
The arachnoid and pia enclose a space filled with cerebrospinal fluid.
The fluid cushions the brain and reduces its effective weight from 1,400 g to about 50 g.
The blood-brain barrier filters what passes from blood into brain tissue.
blocks.end: The ventricles produce about half a litre of fluid every day.

items: MRI
Magnetic fields and radio waves produce detailed images of structure without radiation.
PET
Tracks radioactive tracers to show where the brain uses glucose or blood flow increases.
fMRI
Measures changes in blood oxygen to show which regions are active during a task.
blocks.end: CT scanning uses X-rays from many angles and is still the fastest scan for a suspected stroke.

blocks.text: The retina is part of the brain. It forms as an outgrowth of the embryonic forebrain, which is why an eye exam is the only way to see central nervous tissue without surgery.

entries.title: The Eye
entries.what: The eye focuses light onto the retina, a thin sheet of neural tissue where photoreceptors turn light into electrical signals and ganglion cells send the result to the brain.
entries.gives: Vision supplies most of what we know about the world around us. The retina also shows, in miniature, how every sensory system filters and simplifies its input.
entries.pic: An eye from the side: light enters at the front and lands on the bronze retina at the back.

steps.t: Close your left eye and look at a single point on a wall with your right.
Hold a pen at arm's length to the right of that point and move it slowly outward.
At about 15 degrees, the tip disappears. This is the blind spot, where the optic nerve leaves the eye.
Go into a dark room and wait.
Over 20 to 30 minutes, rod photoreceptors slowly regain sensitivity. This is dark adaptation.
Look directly at a dim star at night, then just beside it.
It appears brighter off-centre, because the centre of the retina has cones only and no rods.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 9: The Eye

words.meaning: A small pit at the centre of the retina with tightly packed cones, giving the sharpest vision.
The chain of chemical steps by which a photoreceptor converts light into a change in charge.
The area of the visual field where light changes a given cell's firing.

blocks.h: A camera that edits its own image
paras: The cornea and lens bend light so that it lands in focus on the retina at the back of the eye. The cornea does most of the bending. The lens adjusts for distance by changing shape, a process called accommodation.

The retina is built in an unexpected order. Light passes through layers of neurons before reaching the photoreceptors at the back. Signals then travel forward again, from photoreceptors to bipolar cells to ganglion cells, whose axons form the optic nerve.
About 125 million photoreceptors feed only about one million ganglion cells. The retina therefore compresses the image heavily, reporting edges and contrast rather than absolute brightness.

items: Cornea
The clear front surface. It provides about two thirds of the eye's focusing power.
Lens
Changes shape to focus near or far. It stiffens with age, which is why reading glasses become necessary.
Pupil
Opens and closes to control light. Its size also changes depth of field, like a camera aperture.
Myopia
Short-sightedness: the eye is too long, so distant images focus in front of the retina.
Hyperopia
Long-sightedness: the eye is too short, so near objects focus behind the retina.
Pupillary reflex
Light in one eye constricts both pupils. Doctors use it to check brainstem function.

blocks.h: Two systems for two kinds of light
items: Rods
About 90 million per eye. Highly sensitive and used in dim light. They do not distinguish colour.
Cones
About 5 million per eye, concentrated in the fovea. They work in daylight and give sharp, colour vision.
Three cone types
Each responds best to blue, green or red wavelengths. Colour is computed from the ratio of their signals.
blocks.end: Most colour blindness comes from a missing or altered red or green cone pigment, and is far more common in men.

items: In the dark, sodium channels in the photoreceptor stay open. The cell is relatively charged and releases glutamate steadily.
Light changes the shape of the pigment rhodopsin.
This activates a G-protein cascade that lowers the level of cyclic GMP.
Sodium channels close and the photoreceptor becomes more negative.
Glutamate release falls. In the visual system, light reduces transmitter output.
blocks.end: One activated pigment molecule can close hundreds of channels, which makes rods sensitive to single photons.

items: ON and OFF cells
ON-centre cells fire when light falls on the centre of their field; OFF-centre cells fire when it is removed.
Centre and surround
The surround has the opposite effect to the centre, so cells respond best to contrast, not even light.
M and P types
Large M-type cells signal motion and coarse shape. Smaller P-type cells signal fine detail and colour.

blocks.text: Some ganglion cells contain their own light pigment, melanopsin. They do not help with seeing; they tell the brain's daily clock whether it is day or night, and work even in some people who are otherwise blind.

entries.title: From Eye to Brain
entries.what: Signals from each eye travel through the optic chiasm and thalamus to the primary visual cortex at the back of the brain, where the image is broken down into edges, orientations and colours.
entries.gives: This pathway explains why damage in different places causes very different kinds of visual loss, and how the brain begins to build a picture from simple parts.
entries.pic: Two eyes, the crossing point behind them and the road to the back of the head.

steps.t: Look straight ahead and hold your arms out to the sides.
Wiggle the fingers of your left hand while keeping your eyes fixed forward.
Everything in your left visual field is processed by the right hemisphere, and the reverse.
Cover one eye, then the other, while looking at the same point.
Each eye sees most of both fields. Fibres from the inner half of each retina cross at the chiasm.
Look at a vertical line, then a tilted one.
Different groups of cells in primary visual cortex respond to each orientation.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 10: The Central Visual System

words.meaning: The crossing point under the brain where fibres from the inner half of each retina switch sides.
The lateral geniculate nucleus: the thalamic relay between retina and visual cortex.
The property of a visual cortex cell that fires most to an edge at one particular angle.

blocks.h: The route from retina to cortex
paras: The optic nerves meet under the brain at the chiasm. Fibres from the half of each retina nearest the nose cross over; the rest stay on the same side. As a result, each half of the brain receives the opposite half of the visual world from both eyes.

About 90 percent of the fibres go to the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus. The rest go to the hypothalamus for daily rhythms, the pretectum for pupil control and the superior colliculus for eye movements.
From the thalamus, signals reach primary visual cortex, also called V1 or striate cortex. Here, cells stop responding to spots of light and start responding to lines and edges at particular angles.

items: Optic nerve
Damage to one nerve causes blindness in that eye only.
Optic chiasm
Pressure here, often from a pituitary tumour, removes the outer visual field on both sides, leaving tunnel vision.
Optic tract
Damage behind the chiasm removes the opposite half of the visual field in both eyes.
blocks.end: A neurologist can often locate a lesion from the pattern of visual loss alone.

items: Six layers
Stacked like bent pancakes. Each layer receives from one eye only.
Eye segregation
Layers 1, 4 and 6 receive from the opposite eye; layers 2, 3 and 5 from the same-side eye.
Magno layers
The two bottom layers receive from M-type ganglion cells: motion and coarse form.
Parvo layers
The four top layers receive from P-type cells: fine detail and red-green colour.
Konio layers
Thin layers between the others carry blue-yellow colour information.
Feedback
About 80 percent of its excitatory input comes back from the cortex, not the eye.
V1 lies at the back of the occipital lobe and holds a map of the visual field, with the centre greatly enlarged.
It is about 2 mm thick and arranged in six main layers. Input from the thalamus arrives in layer IV.
Columns of cells prefer input from one eye or the other, in alternating stripes about half a millimetre wide.
Neighbouring columns prefer edges at gradually shifting angles, forming a full 180 degree cycle.
Patches rich in the enzyme cytochrome oxidase, called blobs, handle colour.
blocks.end: Hubel and Wiesel mapped this structure in the 1960s and 70s and shared the Nobel Prize in 1981.

items: Simple cells
Respond to an edge at one angle and one exact position, built from lined-up thalamic inputs.
Complex cells
Respond to an edge at one angle anywhere within a wider area. Many also prefer one direction of motion.
Binocular cells
Above layer IV, most cells receive from both eyes, which is the basis of depth perception.

entries.title: Beyond the First Stop
entries.what: Beyond primary visual cortex, two streams carry visual information onward: a dorsal stream toward the parietal lobe for motion and action, and a ventral stream toward the temporal lobe for recognising objects and faces.
entries.gives: These streams explain why some brain injuries remove the ability to see motion, colour or faces while leaving the rest of vision intact.
entries.pic: The back of the brain with two arrows: one along the bottom, one up over the top.

steps.t: Watch a person walk across the room.
Notice that you see motion as one smooth event.
Area MT in the dorsal stream computes direction and speed of movement.
Look at a familiar face, then at a familiar object.
Different regions in the ventral stream respond more strongly to each.
Look at a coloured object in dim light.
Colour fades as cones lose sensitivity, but shape remains. Colour and form use partly separate routes.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 10: The Central Visual System

words.meaning: A region in the dorsal stream where nearly every cell responds to motion in a particular direction.
Inferior temporal cortex: the end of the ventral stream, involved in object recognition and visual memory.
An inability to recognise faces despite otherwise normal vision.

paras: Beyond V1 lie more than two dozen visual areas, each with its own map of the visual field. They are not arranged in a single line. Two broad streams stand out, each fed mostly by different channels from V1.

The dorsal stream runs up toward the parietal lobe. It extends the magno pathway and specialises in motion, spatial position and guiding action. The ventral stream runs down toward the temporal lobe and extends the parvo and blob pathways, handling shape, colour and identity.
Perception does not depend on a single final cell. It emerges from many broadly tuned areas working in parallel, closer to an orchestra than an assembly line.

items: Area MT
Almost all cells respond to motion in a specific direction, arranged in direction columns like orientation columns in V1.
Area MST
Cells respond to complex motion: expanding, contracting or rotating patterns, useful when moving through space.
Causal evidence
Weak stimulation of an MT column in monkeys shifts which direction of motion they report seeing.
In 1983, a woman in Munich had a stroke that damaged motion areas on both sides of her brain.
Her vision for colour, shape and depth remained largely normal.
Pouring coffee, she saw it frozen in the cup, then suddenly overflowing.
Crossing a road, cars seemed far away, then suddenly next to her.
The condition, akinetopsia, shows that motion has its own dedicated processing.
blocks.end: Motion is not inferred from snapshots. The brain computes it directly.

items: Area V4
Cells are selective for both colour and shape. Damage nearby can cause achromatopsia, a loss of colour vision with healthy cones.
Area IT
Cells respond to complex shapes and objects. It is also important for visual memory.
Face cells
A small share of IT cells respond strongly to faces. In humans, a matching region lights up on fMRI.

blocks.h: Is one cell enough to recognise a person?
items: The idea
Perhaps a handful of neurons fire only to one specific person, such as your grandmother.
No evidence
Recordings across the monkey brain show no area with cells for each of the millions of objects we know.
Broad tuning
Every level of the visual system uses cells that respond to a range of inputs, not one.
Many properties
A cell tuned to one feature also responds to others, such as size and motion.
Fragility
If a memory relied on five cells, a small injury could erase a person entirely.
The alternative
Recognition likely depends on patterns of activity spread across large groups of cells.

blocks.text: Random-dot stereograms show no visible shape to either eye alone. A square appears only when the brain fuses the two images, proving that depth can be computed before objects are recognised.

entries.title: Hearing
entries.what: The ear converts pressure waves in air into fluid waves in the cochlea, where hair cells turn vibration into electrical signals. A separate set of organs in the inner ear senses balance and head motion.
entries.gives: Hearing supports speech and music, and the balance system keeps vision stable while the head moves. Damage to either is common and often preventable.
entries.pic: A coiled tube. The wide bronze base takes high notes, the narrow tip low notes.

steps.t: Sit in a quiet room and close your eyes.
Snap your fingers to the left of your head, then the right.
You locate the sound from tiny differences in arrival time and loudness between your two ears.
Hum a low note, then a high one.
Low frequencies vibrate the far end of the cochlea; high frequencies vibrate the near end.
Shake your head side to side while reading a line of text.
The text stays readable. The vestibular system moves your eyes against your head automatically.

entries.safety: Prolonged exposure above 85 decibels damages hair cells permanently. Keep headphone volume moderate.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 11: The Auditory and Vestibular Systems

words.meaning: The snail-shaped, fluid-filled part of the inner ear that turns sound into nerve signals.
The sensory cell of the ear. Bending its tiny hairs opens channels and changes its charge.
An orderly map of sound frequency, found from the cochlea all the way to auditory cortex.

blocks.h: From air to fluid to nerve
paras: Sound is a pattern of pressure waves in air. Frequency sets pitch and amplitude sets loudness. Humans hear roughly 20 to 20,000 cycles per second, with the range narrowing at the high end with age.

The outer ear funnels sound to the eardrum. Three small bones in the middle ear pass the vibration to the oval window of the cochlea. Because the eardrum is much larger than the window, pressure is concentrated about twenty times, overcoming the resistance of fluid.

Inside the cochlea, the basilar membrane vibrates at different points for different frequencies. Hair cells along it convert that motion into electrical signals, sent through the auditory nerve to the brainstem.

items: Pinna
The visible outer ear. Its folds alter sound slightly depending on whether it comes from above or below.
Eardrum
A thin membrane that vibrates with incoming pressure waves.
Ossicles
Malleus, incus and stapes: the three smallest bones in the body, linked as a lever system.
Attenuation reflex
Muscles stiffen the ossicles in response to loud sounds, protecting the inner ear from sustained noise.
Cochlea
A coiled tube of three fluid chambers. Unrolled, it is about 32 mm long.
Eustachian tube
Connects the middle ear to the throat and equalises pressure when you swallow.
Inner hair cells
About 3,500 per ear in a single row. They send nearly all the information to the brain.
Outer hair cells
About 12,000 in three rows. They change length with each vibration, amplifying the motion of the membrane.
Transduction
Bending the hairs pulls tiny linking filaments that open channels directly, faster than any chemical cascade.
blocks.end: Outer hair cells are so active that the ear can emit faint sounds of its own, used to screen newborn hearing.

blocks.h: How the brain finds a source
items: For low frequencies, the brain compares arrival times. A sound from the left reaches the left ear up to 0.6 ms earlier.
For high frequencies, the head casts a sound shadow, so the far ear hears it more quietly.
Neurons in the superior olive in the brainstem compare input from both ears.
For height, the brain reads how the pinna reshapes the sound.
The result is a map of sound location used to orient the eyes and head.
blocks.end: A one-ear injury makes horizontal localisation much harder.

items: Otolith organs
The utricle and saccule contain small calcium crystals that sense gravity and straight-line acceleration.
Semicircular canals
Three fluid-filled loops at right angles to each other sense rotation of the head in any direction.
Vestibulo-ocular reflex
Moves the eyes opposite to head motion within about 10 ms, keeping the image steady.
Conductive loss
Sound cannot reach the cochlea, often from fluid, wax or stiff ossicles. Usually treatable.
Sensorineural loss
Damage to hair cells or the auditory nerve, often from noise or ageing. Usually permanent.
Cochlear implant
Electrodes inserted along the cochlea stimulate the nerve directly, bypassing lost hair cells.
blocks.end: Tinnitus, a ringing without sound, often follows hair cell damage.

entries.title: Smell and Taste
entries.what: Taste and smell are chemical senses. Taste detects five basic qualities on the tongue; smell detects thousands of airborne molecules in the nose. Together they create flavour.
entries.gives: These are the oldest senses. They protect against spoiled food and toxins, shape appetite and connect directly to memory and emotion.
entries.pic: A tongue with a taste bud, and a nose above it with a bronze smell receptor.

steps.t: Take a jelly bean or a piece of fruit and pinch your nose shut.
Chew slowly and note what you taste.
You detect sweetness and sourness but not the specific flavour. That comes from smell.
Release your nose while still chewing.
Flavour arrives at once, as aroma travels from the back of the mouth up to the nose.
Smell a familiar scent from childhood.
Smell signals reach memory and emotion areas without first passing through the thalamus.

entries.safety: Use only foods you know are safe for you.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 8: The Chemical Senses

words.meaning: The sense of taste.
The sense of smell.
A small cluster in the olfactory bulb where all receptor cells of one type converge.

paras: Even bacteria swim toward food and away from poisons by detecting chemicals. In humans, chemical sensing has expanded into two separate systems. Taste tells us whether something in the mouth is safe and nourishing; smell samples the air for distant information.

Taste has five basic qualities: salty, sour, sweet, bitter and umami, the savoury taste of amino acids like glutamate. Each is sensed by cells in taste buds on the tongue, palate and throat. The idea of a tongue map with separate zones is a myth.

Smell is far richer. Humans have about 350 working odorant receptor types and can tell apart thousands of odours. Each odour activates a unique combination of receptors, read by the brain like a chord.

items: Salty
Sodium enters taste cells directly through dedicated sodium channels.
Sour
Acids release hydrogen ions, which change the cell's charge.
Bitter
About 30 receptor types detect a wide range of plant toxins. Sensitivity is very high.
Sweet
One receptor made of two subunits detects sugars and artificial sweeteners.
Umami
A related receptor detects glutamate, found in meat, cheese and tomatoes.
Taste buds
Each holds 50 to 150 receptor cells. They are replaced about every two weeks.
Three cranial nerves carry taste from different parts of the mouth.
They converge on the gustatory nucleus in the medulla.
Signals pass to the thalamus, then to primary gustatory cortex near the insula.
Branches also reach the hypothalamus and amygdala, linking taste to appetite and emotion.
Each taste cell is tuned to one quality, and its path to the brain is largely separate.
blocks.end: A single bad experience with a food can create a lasting aversion, even when the cause was something else.

items: Receptor neurons
About 10 million per nose, in a patch of tissue high in the nasal cavity. They are replaced every four to eight weeks.
Receptor genes
Mice have about 1,000 odorant receptor genes, humans about 350 functional ones. Each neuron expresses only one.
Transduction
An odorant binds its receptor, triggering a G-protein cascade that opens channels and fires the neuron.
blocks.end: Buck and Axel discovered the odorant receptor family and shared the Nobel Prize in 2004.

items: Receptor axons pass through small holes in the skull to the olfactory bulb.
All neurons with the same receptor converge on one or two glomeruli, about 2,000 in each bulb.
Each odour creates a distinct spatial pattern across the glomeruli.
Bulb output reaches olfactory cortex, the amygdala and areas near the hippocampus.
Some routes bypass the thalamus, unlike every other sense.
blocks.end: This direct link to emotion and memory explains why smells can recall events so vividly.

entries.title: Movement I
entries.what: Every movement is executed by motor neurons in the spinal cord and brainstem that drive skeletal muscle. Spinal circuits handle reflexes and rhythms on their own.
entries.gives: The spinal cord does far more than relay commands. It adjusts force, protects muscles and produces walking patterns without the brain's detailed involvement.
entries.pic: A leg bent at the knee, a bronze tap below the kneecap and a loop to the spinal cord.

steps.t: Sit on a high chair with one leg hanging freely.
Tap just below the kneecap with the side of your hand.
The leg kicks. A stretch sensor in the thigh muscle triggers motor neurons directly, through one synapse.
Lift a light object, then a heavy one.
More motor units and faster firing rates produce the extra force.
Step on something sharp in your mind.
The foot withdraws while the other leg stiffens to take your weight. Spinal circuits coordinate both.

entries.safety: Tap gently, and skip the tap if your knee is injured.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 13: Spinal Control of Movement

words.meaning: One alpha motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it controls.
A sensor inside the muscle that reports how stretched the muscle is.
A spinal circuit that produces rhythmic movement, such as walking, without rhythmic input.

paras: Everything we do, from whispering to running, is carried out by muscle. Around 700 skeletal muscles are controlled by alpha motor neurons in the spinal cord and brainstem. These neurons are the only route from the nervous system to movement.

An alpha motor neuron and the muscle fibres it controls form a motor unit. Small units with a few fibres allow fine control in the fingers and eyes. Large units with thousands of fibres produce force in the legs and back.

The spinal cord also contains circuits that work without the brain. They manage reflexes, balance opposing muscles and produce the basic rhythm of walking. The brain mainly selects, starts and adjusts these programmes.

items: Firing rate
Faster firing lets twitches overlap and fuse into a sustained, stronger contraction.
Recruitment
Small motor units are activated first, then larger ones, so force increases smoothly.
Fibre types
Slow units resist fatigue and support posture. Fast units produce strong but brief bursts.
blocks.end: Training and use can shift a muscle's fibre types, because the nerve shapes the muscle it controls.

items: Acetylcholine released at the neuromuscular junction triggers a spike in the muscle fibre.
The spike travels into the fibre along T-tubules.
Calcium is released from internal stores.
Calcium lets myosin heads grab actin filaments and pull them past each other.
ATP releases the grip. Without it, muscles lock, which causes rigor after death.
blocks.end: This is called the sliding filament mechanism.

items: Muscle spindles
Lie parallel to muscle fibres and fire when the muscle is stretched.
Stretch reflex
Spindle signals excite motor neurons of the same muscle directly. The knee jerk is the classic example.
Gamma motor neurons
Adjust spindle tension so they stay sensitive as the muscle shortens.
Golgi tendon organs
Sit in tendons and report muscle tension, protecting against overload.
Reciprocal inhibition
When one muscle contracts, interneurons relax its opposing muscle.
Crossed extensor reflex
When one leg withdraws from pain, the other extends to support the body.

blocks.h: Diseases of motor neurons and muscle
items: ALS
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis destroys motor neurons, causing progressive weakness and paralysis.
Myasthenia gravis
The immune system attacks acetylcholine receptors at the muscle, causing fatigue and weakness.
Muscular dystrophy
Duchenne type is caused by loss of the protein dystrophin, so muscle fibres degenerate.

entries.title: Movement II
entries.what: The brain controls movement in three levels: strategy in the association cortex and basal ganglia, tactics in motor cortex and cerebellum, and execution in the brainstem and spinal cord.
entries.gives: This hierarchy explains movement disorders such as Parkinson's and Huntington's disease, and why practice turns effort into automatic skill.
entries.pic: A brain with the motor strip in bronze, the basal ganglia deep inside and the cerebellum below.

steps.t: Reach for a cup on the table.
Notice the decision to reach.
Strategy: frontal and parietal cortex select the goal and the plan.
Notice the path your arm takes.
Tactics: motor cortex and cerebellum set the sequence and timing of muscle contractions.
Notice your grip adjust as you lift.
Execution: brainstem and spinal cord carry out the plan and correct it using feedback.

entries.safety: Move your head gently and stop if you feel dizzy.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 14: Brain Control of Movement

words.meaning: Deep forebrain nuclei that help select and start wanted movements and suppress unwanted ones.
Primary motor cortex, in front of the central sulcus. It holds a map of the body.
The structure at the back of the brain that coordinates timing and corrects errors in movement.

paras: A baseball pitcher shows all three levels. Choosing a pitch is strategy. Planning the arm's path and timing is tactics. Contracting the right muscles in the right order is execution. Each level uses sensory feedback to stay on target.

Commands travel from the brain to the spinal cord in two main groups of tracts. The lateral pathways, led by the corticospinal tract, control voluntary movement of the limbs. The ventromedial pathways control posture and balance.
Two large loops refine every movement. The basal ganglia help choose which action to start. The cerebellum compares intended movement with actual movement and corrects the difference.

items: Corticospinal tract
About one million axons from motor cortex, crossing at the base of the brainstem. It controls fine finger movement.
Rubrospinal tract
A smaller pathway from the midbrain that also controls the limbs.
Ventromedial tracts
From the brainstem: vestibular, tectal and reticular tracts that maintain posture and orient the head.
blocks.end: Damage to the corticospinal tract often causes the Babinski sign, an upward toe response to stroking the sole.

items: Posterior parietal
Combines vision, touch and body position to build a map of where things are relative to the body.
Prefrontal cortex
Holds goals and selects actions. Damage leaves people unable to plan or follow through.
Premotor areas
Neurons fire up to a second before movement, signalling intention rather than muscle activity.
Primary motor cortex
Holds a body map. Hands and face take up far more area than the trunk.
Population coding
Each M1 neuron prefers one direction. Direction is read from the combined vote of many cells.
Flexible map
The motor map reorganises after injury or practice, expanding areas in heavy use.
Cortex sends input to the striatum, made of the caudate and putamen.
Output passes through the globus pallidus to the thalamus and back to the cortex.
At rest, this loop holds movement back. Activation releases the chosen action.
In Parkinson's disease, loss of dopamine cells leaves the brake on: slow, stiff movement and tremor.
In Huntington's disease, loss of striatal cells removes the brake: involuntary, writhing movements.
blocks.end: L-dopa and deep brain stimulation both act on this loop.

items: Structure
Contains about half of all neurons in the brain, arranged in a highly regular circuit.
Role
Compares the command sent with the movement made and adjusts the next one. Essential for smooth, accurate action.
Damage
Causes ataxia: clumsy, poorly timed movements, overshooting targets and a broad, unsteady walk.
blocks.end: Alcohol affects the cerebellum early, which is why roadside sobriety tests check balance and coordination.

entries.title: Brain Chemistry
entries.what: Beyond fast point-to-point signalling, the brain uses three slower systems to set its overall state: hormones from the hypothalamus, the autonomic nervous system and diffuse modulatory systems that bathe whole regions in transmitters.
entries.gives: These systems govern stress, arousal, mood and sleep. They are the main targets of psychiatric medication and of most recreational drugs.
entries.pic: The hypothalamus above the pituitary, with a bronze drop of hormone going into the blood.

steps.t: Recall a moment of sudden alarm, such as a near-miss on the road.
Notice the racing heart and dry mouth.
The sympathetic nervous system acts within seconds, releasing norepinephrine to heart and vessels.
Notice that the tension lasts for minutes.
The hypothalamus has triggered cortisol release through the pituitary and adrenal glands.
Notice your attention narrowing.
The locus coeruleus has raised norepinephrine across the cortex, sharpening vigilance.

entries.safety: Stand up slowly if you feel light-headed.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 15: Chemical Control of the Brain and Behavior

words.meaning: The regulation of internal conditions, such as temperature and blood chemistry, within a narrow range.
The part of the nervous system that controls organs, glands and blood vessels without conscious effort.
A small group of neurons with widely branching axons that adjusts the activity of large brain regions.

blocks.h: Setting the state of the whole brain
paras: Most synapses are narrow and fast, linking one neuron to a few others. But some signals need to reach many targets at once and last longer. The brain uses three systems for this, each slower and broader than the last.

The hypothalamus, a structure the size of a grape, controls the pituitary gland and through it most of the body's hormones. It also runs the autonomic nervous system, which adjusts heart rate, digestion and blood flow.

Finally, a few thousand neurons in the brainstem and forebrain send axons across the entire brain. They release norepinephrine, serotonin, dopamine and acetylcholine, setting levels of alertness, mood and motivation.

items: Posterior pituitary
Neurons release oxytocin and vasopressin directly into the blood. Vasopressin controls water balance.
Anterior pituitary
Hypothalamic releasing hormones travel through local blood vessels and trigger pituitary hormones.
Stress axis
The hypothalamus, pituitary and adrenal glands together release cortisol, which mobilises fuel.
Feedback
Cortisol acts back on the brain to switch off the stress response once the threat passes.
Chronic stress
Sustained high cortisol can damage hippocampal neurons and impair memory.
Homeostasis
Monitors temperature, blood sugar and salt, then corrects them through hormones and behaviour.
Sympathetic
Prepares the body for action: raises heart rate, widens pupils and airways, slows digestion. Uses norepinephrine at its targets.
Parasympathetic
Supports rest and digestion: slows the heart, stimulates digestion and saliva. Uses acetylcholine at its targets.
Enteric
A network of about 500 million neurons in the gut wall that runs digestion largely on its own.

blocks.h: Four groups that shape the whole brain
items: Norepinephrine: the locus coeruleus, about 12,000 neurons per side, raises alertness to new and important events.
Serotonin: the raphe nuclei regulate sleep and waking, mood and some aspects of emotional behaviour.
Dopamine: the substantia nigra supports movement; the ventral tegmental area supports reward and motivation.
Acetylcholine: the basal forebrain supports attention, learning and memory.
Each group is small, but a single neuron can contact over 250,000 others.
blocks.end: Loss of basal forebrain acetylcholine neurons is one of the earliest changes in Alzheimer's disease.

items: Hallucinogens
LSD and psilocybin act on serotonin receptors in the cortex, altering perception and thought.
Stimulants
Cocaine and amphetamine increase dopamine and norepinephrine, raising alertness and confidence.
Dependence
Repeated use alters the systems involved, so normal function comes to require the drug.

entries.title: When the Brain Is Unwell
entries.what: Mental illnesses are disorders of brain function influenced by genes, development and experience. Anxiety disorders, mood disorders and schizophrenia are the most studied, and each has effective treatments.
entries.gives: Seeing mental illness as a brain condition reduces stigma, guides treatment and explains why medication and therapy both work.
entries.pic: A healthy neuron next to one with bronze clumps outside and tangles inside.

steps.t: Pick one condition, such as depression.
Ask what it looks like in behaviour and experience.
Persistent low mood, loss of interest, poor sleep and appetite, lasting at least two weeks.
Ask what is known about its biology.
Genes raise vulnerability. Stress and a dysregulated cortisol response often act as triggers.
Ask how it is treated.
Psychotherapy, medication, or both. Each changes brain function, and they work best together.

entries.safety: This topic is educational. For any mental health concern, speak with a doctor or qualified therapist.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 22: Mental Illness

words.meaning: A medication that reduces anxiety, such as a benzodiazepine.
The idea that illness arises from an inherited vulnerability combined with environmental stress.
A medication that reduces psychotic symptoms, mostly by blocking dopamine D2 receptors.

blocks.h: Illness of the brain, not of character
paras: For much of history, mental illness was blamed on spirits, weak will or poor upbringing. Modern evidence shows that it arises from the same kinds of processes as other brain conditions: genes, development, chemistry and experience acting together.

Two approaches complement each other. The psychosocial approach looks at life history, thought patterns and relationships. The biological approach looks at genes, circuits and transmitters. Both are needed for a full picture.
No single gene causes these disorders. Many genes each add a small amount of risk. Whether illness develops often depends on stress, timing and environment.

items: Panic disorder
Sudden attacks of intense fear with a pounding heart, breathlessness and a sense of doom, often without a trigger.
Agoraphobia
Fear of places where escape is hard. It often develops after panic attacks and can confine people to their homes.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder
Intrusive thoughts and repeated rituals to relieve them, linked to overactive frontal-basal ganglia loops.
The amygdala detects threat and activates the hypothalamus.
The hypothalamus triggers cortisol release through the pituitary and adrenal glands.
The hippocampus normally senses cortisol and switches the response off.
Chronic stress weakens hippocampal control and strengthens the amygdala.
The result is a stress system stuck in the on position.
blocks.end: Benzodiazepines calm this circuit by strengthening GABA inhibition; SSRIs also reduce anxiety over weeks.

items: Major depression
Low mood, loss of pleasure, poor sleep, guilt and fatigue for at least two weeks. Affects about one in five people over a lifetime.
Bipolar disorder
Episodes of depression alternate with mania: elevated mood, little sleep, racing thoughts and risky decisions.
Monoamine theory
Many antidepressants raise norepinephrine or serotonin, suggesting a role for these systems.
The delay
Antidepressants raise transmitter levels within hours, but mood improves only after weeks of slower brain changes.
Lithium
A simple salt that stabilises mood in bipolar disorder. Its exact mechanism is still being studied.
ECT
Electroconvulsive therapy, given under anaesthesia, remains one of the most effective treatments for severe depression.

blocks.h: A disorder of perception and thought
items: Symptoms
Hallucinations, delusions and disorganised thinking, along with reduced motivation and emotional expression.
Dopamine hypothesis
Drugs that block dopamine D2 receptors reduce psychosis; drugs that raise dopamine can produce it.
Glutamate hypothesis
Drugs that block NMDA glutamate receptors, such as PCP, mimic the full range of symptoms.
blocks.end: Onset is usually in late teens or early twenties. Genes and early environment both raise risk.

entries.title: Motivation
entries.what: Motivation is the drive that turns needs into action. The hypothalamus monitors body states such as fuel and temperature, and dopamine circuits assign value to the actions that satisfy them.
entries.gives: Understanding motivation explains hunger and fullness, body weight regulation and why addictive drugs take over behaviour.
entries.pic: A balance scale in the middle of the brain, with a bronze weight on one side.

steps.t: Before a meal, notice your hunger level on a scale of one to ten.
Eat slowly and check again halfway through.
Stretch receptors in the stomach and gut hormones such as CCK have begun signalling fullness.
Wait twenty minutes after finishing.
Fullness grows as insulin and other signals reach the hypothalamus.
Notice whether you still want dessert.
Wanting is driven partly by dopamine and can continue after the body's need is met.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 16: Motivation

words.meaning: A hormone released by fat cells that tells the brain how much fuel is stored.
The feeling of fullness that ends a meal.
Two components of reward: the drive toward something (dopamine) and the pleasure it gives (opioids).

paras: Behaviour has a direction. Some drives are concrete, such as hunger, thirst or cold. Others are abstract, such as the urge to finish a project. In each case, the brain detects a gap between how things are and how they should be, and pushes behaviour to close it.

The hypothalamus is the main sensor for body needs. It tracks stored fuel, blood sugar, salt and temperature. When values drift, it triggers three responses: hormones, autonomic changes and motivated behaviour.

Dopamine circuits add value. They mark which actions and cues lead to reward, so that we pursue them again. The same circuits can be hijacked by drugs, which produce strong wanting without meeting any real need.

blocks.h: How the brain tracks stored fuel
items: Leptin
Fat cells release leptin in proportion to their size. High leptin reduces appetite and raises metabolic rate.
Low leptin
When fat stores fall, leptin drops. The hypothalamus increases hunger and slows metabolism to conserve fuel.
Lesion studies
Damage to one part of the hypothalamus causes overeating; damage to another causes refusal to eat.
blocks.end: Mice lacking the leptin gene grow to three times normal weight. Leptin injections reverse this in them, but rarely help human obesity.

blocks.h: Why a meal starts and stops
items: Ghrelin from the empty stomach rises before meals and stimulates hunger.
Seeing and smelling food triggers saliva, insulin and stomach acid in advance.
Stretch of the stomach sends fullness signals through the vagus nerve.
CCK released from the gut by fatty food signals satiety.
Insulin from the pancreas rises as glucose is absorbed and reduces further eating.
blocks.end: These signals end a meal. Leptin sets how much is eaten over weeks.

items: Self-stimulation
Rats press a lever thousands of times an hour to stimulate dopamine pathways in their brain.
Wanting, not liking
Dopamine drives the pursuit of a reward. Pleasure itself depends more on opioid and other systems.
Prediction
Dopamine cells fire most to unexpected reward and dip when an expected reward fails to arrive.
Addiction
Drugs raise dopamine directly and powerfully, building strong wanting that persists even as pleasure fades.
Serotonin and mood
Carbohydrate-rich food raises brain serotonin, which helps explain cravings during low mood.
Temperature
The hypothalamus triggers shivering, sweating and behaviour such as finding shelter to hold body heat near 37 degrees.

entries.title: Learning and Memory I
entries.what: Memory is not one system. Declarative memory for facts and events depends on the medial temporal lobes and hippocampus; procedural memory for skills and habits depends on the striatum; working memory depends on prefrontal cortex.
entries.gives: These distinctions explain why amnesia can erase new memories while leaving skills intact, and how to support each type of memory.
entries.pic: Two neurons with a thick bronze link between them: fire together, wire together.

steps.t: Recall what you ate for dinner last night.
Notice that you can describe it in words.
That is declarative memory: facts and events, consciously recalled.
Tie a shoelace without thinking about the steps.
That is procedural memory: a skill stored as action, not words.
Hold a phone number in mind for ten seconds without writing it.
That is working memory: a few items held briefly for immediate use.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 24: Memory Systems

words.meaning: Memory for facts and events that can be consciously recalled and stated.
The physical trace of a memory in the brain.
Loss of memory. Anterograde amnesia prevents new memories; retrograde amnesia erases old ones.

paras: A newborn and a Nobel laureate have similar brains at the level of anatomy. The difference is largely what each has learned. Learning is the acquisition of new information; memory is its storage and later retrieval.

Declarative memory covers facts and personal events. It is fast to form and easy to lose. Nondeclarative memory includes skills, habits and conditioned responses. It forms slowly through repetition and is very durable.
Memory also moves through stages. Short-term memory lasts seconds to minutes and is easily disrupted. Consolidation then turns some of it into long-term memory, a process that can take days to years.

items: In the 1920s, Lashley removed parts of rat cortex and found that maze memory faded with the amount removed, not its location.
He concluded memories are spread widely, not stored in one place.
Hebb proposed that a memory is a cell assembly: a group of neurons whose connections strengthen when they fire together.
Penfield stimulated the temporal lobes of awake patients during surgery. Some reported vivid recollections.
Today, memories are seen as distributed but relying on specific structures to form.
blocks.end: Neurons that fire together strengthen their connections. This principle is still central.

blocks.h: The patient who changed memory research
items: The surgery
In 1953, at age 27, H.M. had both medial temporal lobes removed to treat severe epilepsy.
The result
His seizures improved, but he could no longer form new declarative memories. Each day began without yesterday.
What remained
His intelligence, older memories and ability to learn new motor skills were preserved.
blocks.end: He improved at mirror drawing over days while having no memory of practising.

items: Hippocampus
Binds the parts of an event into one memory and is essential for forming new declarative memories.
Place cells
Hippocampal neurons that fire when an animal is in a particular location, forming a map of space.
Diencephalon
Damage to parts of the thalamus and mammillary bodies, as in Korsakoff's syndrome, also causes amnesia.
Neocortex
Long-term store for consolidated memories, especially in the temporal lobes.
Striatum
Supports habit learning: gradual links between a cue and a response.
Prefrontal cortex
Holds information in working memory and organises retrieval.
Capacity
Holds roughly four to seven items for a few seconds without rehearsal.
Prefrontal neurons
Keep firing during a delay, maintaining information until it is used.
Area LIP
Neurons in parietal cortex hold the location of a remembered target for an upcoming eye movement.

entries.title: Attention
entries.what: Attention is the selective processing of some information over the rest. It enhances neural responses to what we attend to and suppresses what we ignore.
entries.gives: Attention shapes what we perceive and remember. Its disorders, from ADHD to neglect after stroke, show how much ordinary experience depends on it.
entries.pic: A field of grey dots with one bronze dot inside a circle of focus.

steps.t: Look at a point straight ahead and keep your eyes still.
Without moving your eyes, shift your attention to an object at the edge of your vision.
You perceive it more clearly. Attention can move independently of gaze.
In a noisy room, focus on one conversation.
Other voices fade, but your own name in another conversation will still catch your attention.
Read a paragraph while music plays.
You notice less of the music. Attention to one sense reduces processing in another.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 21: Attention

words.meaning: Focusing processing on one source of information while ignoring others.
After damage, usually to the right parietal lobe, a person ignores one side of space.
A large thalamic nucleus thought to help direct attention across the cortex.

paras: The senses deliver far more information than the brain can fully process. Attention selects. At a crowded party, it lets you follow one conversation and ignore the rest, yet still catch your name spoken across the room.
Attention can be directed by choice, such as searching for a friend in a crowd, or captured by events, such as a sudden noise. It can focus on a location, a feature such as colour, or a whole object.
In the brain, attention increases the response of neurons to attended stimuli and shrinks their response to distractors. The effect is measurable from early visual cortex onward.

items: Better detection
Faint stimuli at an attended location are detected more often than identical stimuli elsewhere.
Faster reactions
A cue pointing to where a target will appear speeds responses by tens of milliseconds.
Cost of distraction
A misleading cue slows responses, showing that attention has to move.
Damage to the right parietal lobe, often from stroke, can cause neglect of the left side of space.
Patients may eat only the right half of their plate or shave only one side of the face.
Asked to copy a drawing, they reproduce only its right half.
Their eyes work normally. The problem is in attending to that side.
Neglect often improves over weeks to months as the brain recovers.
blocks.end: The right hemisphere appears to attend to both sides; the left mainly to the right.

items: fMRI
Attending to one location increases activity in the matching part of the visual cortex.
PET
Attending to colour or motion raises activity in the areas specialised for each.
Parietal cortex
Neurons respond more strongly to a stimulus when it is the target of attention.
Area V4
Receptive fields shrink around an attended object, filtering out distractors.
Pulvinar
This thalamic nucleus links many visual areas and helps coordinate where attention goes.
Eye movements
Areas that plan eye movements also direct attention. Planning a look shifts attention first.
Features
Inattention, hyperactivity and impulsiveness beyond what is typical for age, affecting school, work and relationships.
Biology
Strongly heritable. Linked to differences in dopamine and norepinephrine systems and in frontal-striatal circuits.
Treatment
Stimulants such as methylphenidate raise dopamine and norepinephrine and improve focus for many people.

entries.title: Learning and Memory II
entries.what: Memories are stored as changes in the strength of synapses. Long-term strengthening (LTP) and weakening (LTD) of synapses, followed by protein synthesis and structural growth, form the cellular basis of learning.
entries.gives: These mechanisms explain why repetition, spacing and sleep improve learning, and they are the targets of research on memory disorders.
entries.pic: A sea slug with its gill, and a bronze arrow showing the gill pulling back.

steps.t: Recall something you learned only once, then something you practised many times.
Compare how clearly each returns.
Repetition strengthens the same synapses again and again, making the trace durable.
Recall a fact learned the night before a good sleep.
Consolidation depends on new proteins, which are made in the hours after learning.
Notice a habit you have stopped noticing, such as a ticking clock.
That is habituation: a simple form of learning based on reduced transmitter release.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 25: Molecular Mechanisms of Learning and Memory

words.meaning: A lasting increase in synaptic strength after strong, repeated activity. Often called long-term strengthening.
A glutamate receptor that opens only when the cell is already active, detecting coincident input.
A protein that switches on genes needed to turn short-term changes into long-term memory.

paras: Hebb predicted in 1949 that memory depends on changes in the strength of connections between neurons. Decades later, experiments confirmed it. A memory is not stored in a single cell but in the pattern of strengthened and weakened synapses across many cells.

Simple animals made the first breakthroughs. The sea slug Aplysia has large, identifiable neurons and simple reflexes that can be trained. Studies of these reflexes showed how learning changes transmitter release at specific synapses.

In mammals, the hippocampus and cerebellum revealed two complementary mechanisms: LTP, which strengthens synapses, and LTD, which weakens them. Both are needed. A system that only strengthens would quickly saturate.

items: Habituation
A repeated, harmless stimulus produces a smaller and smaller response. You stop noticing the hum of a fridge.
Sensitization
A strong or painful stimulus increases responses to other stimuli for a period afterward.
Conditioning
Classical conditioning links two stimuli; instrumental conditioning links an action to its outcome.
Touching the slug's siphon makes it withdraw its gill, a simple protective reflex.
Repeated gentle touch reduces transmitter release from sensory neurons: habituation.
A shock to the tail releases serotonin, which increases transmitter release: sensitization.
With repeated training, new proteins are made and new synapses grow.
Eric Kandel led this work and shared the Nobel Prize in 2000.
blocks.end: Short-term memory changes existing proteins. Long-term memory needs new ones.

items: Trigger
Strong, high-frequency input to hippocampal neurons produces lasting strengthening of their synapses.
Coincidence
NMDA receptors open only when glutamate binds and the cell is already active, matching Hebb's rule.
Calcium
Calcium entering through NMDA receptors activates enzymes, especially CaMKII.
More receptors
CaMKII adds AMPA receptors to the synapse, making it more responsive to glutamate.
Timing
If input arrives just before the cell fires, the synapse strengthens; if just after, it weakens.
Link to memory
Blocking NMDA receptors in rats prevents learning a water maze.
Protein synthesis
Drugs that block protein synthesis just after learning prevent long-term, but not short-term, memory.
CREB
This switch protein activates genes for consolidation. Raising it in animals improves memory.
Structural change
Learning adds and enlarges dendritic spines, physically reshaping connections.
blocks.end: LTD in the cerebellum weakens specific synapses and supports motor learning, such as adapting a reflex.

entries.title: Emotion
entries.what: Emotion involves bodily responses, conscious feelings and behaviour, coordinated by circuits that include the amygdala, hypothalamus and prefrontal cortex.
entries.gives: These circuits explain fear learning, aggression and how emotion shapes decisions, and they underlie anxiety and mood disorders.
entries.pic: An almond-shaped bronze amygdala deep in the brain, with lines out to the body.

steps.t: Recall a moment when something startled you.
Notice which came first: the jump or the feeling of fear.
The body often reacts before conscious fear. A fast route through the amygdala acts within milliseconds.
Notice how quickly you then judged the situation as safe or not.
A slower route through the cortex assesses detail and can calm the response.
Notice any change in your breath or heartbeat.
Bodily changes feed back to the brain and shape the feeling itself.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 18: Brain Mechanisms of Emotion

words.meaning: An almond-shaped structure in the temporal lobe central to fear and emotional learning.
An older term for a group of structures linked to emotion, including the amygdala and hippocampus.
Learning that a neutral cue predicts something harmful, so the cue alone produces fear.

paras: Emotion has two sides. Emotional expression is what can be observed: changes in heart rate, posture, facial expression and behaviour. Emotional experience is the conscious feeling. Animal studies can measure the first; only humans can report the second.

Early theories disagreed about order. One held that we feel afraid because the body reacts. Another held that brain and body react at the same time, independently. Modern evidence supports a mix: bodily signals shape feelings, but are not the whole story.

There is no single emotion centre. Different emotions rely on overlapping circuits. The amygdala is most closely tied to fear, while the prefrontal cortex helps interpret and regulate emotional responses.

items: James-Lange
We feel afraid because we notice our body trembling and our heart racing. Feeling follows the body.
Cannon-Bard
The brain triggers feeling and bodily change at the same time. Emotions remain after the body's signals are cut.
Unconscious emotion
Studies show that faces flashed too briefly to see still activate the amygdala and change behaviour.
Broca named the limbic lobe, a ring of cortex around the brainstem, in 1878.
Papez proposed in 1937 a loop through the hypothalamus, thalamus, cingulate cortex and hippocampus.
In 1848, Phineas Gage survived an iron rod through his frontal lobe. His personality changed sharply.
Monkeys with temporal lobe removal lost fear and showed odd behaviour: the Klüver-Bucy syndrome.
Later work showed the hippocampus is mainly for memory, and the amygdala for emotion.
blocks.end: The term limbic system survives, but its boundaries are debated.

items: Input
Receives information from every sense, both directly from the thalamus and from the cortex.
Fast route
A direct thalamic path gives a quick, rough signal, enough to trigger a startle.
Slow route
A cortical path delivers detail, allowing a more accurate judgement.
Output
Projections to the hypothalamus and brainstem raise heart rate, cortisol and freezing.
Learning
When a tone predicts a shock, synapses in the amygdala strengthen and the tone alone produces fear.
Human damage
People with amygdala damage struggle to recognise fear in faces and show weak fear conditioning.
Hypothalamus
Stimulating different areas produces either defensive rage or calm predatory attack in animals.
Serotonin
Low serotonin activity is linked to impulsive aggression in animals and humans.
Surgery
Amygdala and frontal lobe surgery were once used to reduce aggression. Frontal lobotomy was abandoned for its severe effects.

entries.title: Sleep
entries.what: Sleep is an active, regulated state with two main types, non-REM and REM, cycling through the night. A brain clock in the hypothalamus times sleep and waking to the 24-hour day.
entries.gives: Sleep is essential for health, memory and mood. Understanding it helps explain jet lag, insomnia and disorders such as narcolepsy.
entries.pic: A wave pattern: small fast waves awake, big slow waves in deep sleep, small fast waves again in REM.

steps.t: For one week, note your bedtime and the time you wake naturally.
Notice when you feel most alert and when you feel drowsy.
The suprachiasmatic nucleus sets a daily rhythm of alertness, hormone release and temperature.
Get bright light within an hour of waking.
Morning light resets the clock through special light-sensitive cells in the retina.
Keep the last two hours before bed dim.
Darkness allows melatonin to rise, which signals night to the body.

entries.safety: Persistent poor sleep, loud snoring or sudden daytime sleep should be checked by a doctor.

source.name: Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 3rd edition · Chapter 19: Brain Rhythms and Sleep

words.meaning: Electroencephalogram: a recording of brain electrical rhythms from electrodes on the scalp.
Rapid eye movement sleep: an active brain state with vivid dreams and paralysed muscles.
A small cluster of cells in the hypothalamus that acts as the brain's master clock.

paras: The Earth turns every 24 hours, and nearly every living thing keeps time with it. In humans, the most visible rhythm is sleep and waking. Sleep is not a switching-off. It is a structured state with its own patterns of brain activity.

Brain rhythms are recorded with the EEG. Waking produces fast, irregular, low-amplitude waves. Deep non-REM sleep produces slow, large waves as millions of neurons fire in synchrony. REM sleep looks almost like waking on the EEG, yet the body is paralysed.

Two systems control sleep. A homeostatic drive builds with time awake, partly through adenosine. A circadian clock in the hypothalamus sets the best window for sleep each day. Sleep comes most easily when both align.

items: Beta
Fast waves above 14 per second, seen during alert thinking and attention.
Alpha
8 to 13 per second, seen during relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed.
Theta
4 to 7 per second, seen in drowsiness and some stages of sleep.
Delta
Slow waves below 4 per second, dominant in deep non-REM sleep.
Synchrony
Large waves mean many neurons fire together, often paced by the thalamus.
Epilepsy
Seizures are bursts of excessive synchronous activity, visible as spikes on the EEG.
Stage 1: light sleep for a few minutes, slow rolling eye movements.
Stage 2: sleep spindles and K-complexes appear. About half the night is spent here.
Stages 3 and 4: deep slow-wave sleep. Hardest to wake from; most common early in the night.
REM: rapid eye movements, vivid dreams and paralysis of most muscles.
One cycle takes about 90 minutes. REM periods lengthen toward morning.
blocks.end: Sleepwalking and night terrors occur in deep non-REM sleep, not during dreams.

items: Restoration
Sleep allows the brain and body to recover. Deprived animals lose weight, temperature control and eventually die.
Adaptation
Sleep keeps animals still and safe during hours when activity would be dangerous or wasteful.
Memory
Both slow-wave and REM sleep support consolidation of the day's learning.
blocks.end: A high school student stayed awake for 11 days in 1964. He recovered fully after sleeping, but showed lapses and irritability throughout.

blocks.h: What switches sleep on and off
items: Arousal system
Brainstem and forebrain neurons using norepinephrine, serotonin, acetylcholine and histamine keep the cortex awake.
Sleep switch
A group of hypothalamic neurons inhibits the arousal system to start sleep.
REM control
Acetylcholine neurons in the brainstem trigger REM; the same region blocks motor neurons, paralysing the body.
Adenosine
Builds up during waking and promotes sleep. Caffeine blocks its receptors.
Narcolepsy
Loss of orexin neurons causes sudden sleep attacks and collapse during strong emotion.
Antihistamines
Older types cross into the brain and block histamine, which is why they cause drowsiness.
The clock
The suprachiasmatic nucleus contains about 20,000 neurons. Each cell keeps time through a loop of clock genes.
Free running
Without daylight, the human clock drifts to a cycle slightly longer than 24 hours.
Light input
Light-sensitive ganglion cells with melanopsin reset the clock daily, even in some blind people.
