entries.title: How We Study the Senses
entries.what: The senses are studied with a toolkit: careful behavioural tests, anatomy, recording single cells, stimulation, switching areas off, imaging and light-controlled genes.
entries.gives: Every claim about seeing and hearing in this part rests on one of these methods. Knowing them lets you judge how solid a finding is.
entries.pic: An eye and an ear joined to one brain, with a recording needle in bronze.

steps.t: Pick a small dot on a wall about two metres away and keep your eyes on it.
Hold a coloured pen beside your head and bring it slowly forward from behind.
You notice movement before you can name the colour. The edge of the retina detects change but resolves little detail.
Now read a line of text and pay attention to your eyes.
They move in quick jumps, about three per second. The sharp centre of the eye has to be pointed at each word.

entries.safety: Never look at the sun or a bright lamp, and stop if your eyes strain or water.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.04 Sensory Systems · Introduction and the visual system

words.meaning: Measuring what a person or animal can detect or tell apart, under tightly controlled conditions.
The patch of the visual field, or band of sound frequencies, that changes a given cell's firing.
Placing light-sensitive proteins into chosen cells so that light can switch those cells on or off.

blocks.h: Two senses, one set of questions
paras: Vision and hearing are the two senses we understand best. Both start with receptor cells that turn a physical signal into electrical activity, and both pass that activity through a chain of brain stations before it becomes experience.

The questions are the same for each sense. What does each station add? Which cells carry which kind of information? What is lost when a part is damaged? Answers come from combining several methods, because each one alone can mislead.

The eye maps space directly onto the retina. The ear maps frequency instead, so the brain has to compute where a sound is. That single difference shapes how the two systems are built, and it runs through the whole of this part.

items: Psychophysics
Detection and discrimination tests show exactly what an observer can and cannot see or hear.
Anatomy
Stains reveal cell bodies, whole neurons and the wiring between areas.
Recording
Fine electrodes pick up single cells firing; played on a speaker, you can hear a receptive field.
Stimulation
Current in the visual cortex makes a person see a point of light. In eye-movement areas it moves the eyes.
Inactivation
Lesions, local anaesthetic or reversible cooling show what is lost when an area falls silent.
Imaging and optogenetics
fMRI shows active areas. Light-sensitive proteins switch chosen cell types on or off.
Detection
One target appears. Its contrast, size or colour is lowered until it can no longer be found.
Discrimination
One odd item sits among identical ones. The difference shrinks until the odd one cannot be picked out.
Fixation
The observer holds the gaze on a spot, so each stimulus lands on a known place on the retina.
Outer and middle ear
The eardrum and three tiny bones carry vibration into the fluid-filled inner ear.
Cochlea
A coiled tube where hair cells sit in order: high pitches at the base, low pitches at the tip.
Auditory nerve
About 30,000 fibres per ear, each tuned to its own best frequency, carry the signal to the brainstem.

entries.title: From Eye to Cortex
entries.what: The thalamus relays each eye's signal in separate layers to the primary visual cortex, where cells start to respond to edges, their orientation, direction of motion and the input of both eyes.
entries.gives: This is where the visual image is first taken apart into features. The same principles of columns and maps appear across the cortex.
entries.pic: Six stacked layers in the thalamus feeding a striped sheet of cortex, one stripe in bronze.

steps.t: Hold a pencil upright at arm's length and look at it.
Tilt it slowly through a full half-turn.
Each angle drives a different group of cells in the primary visual cortex. You notice even a small tilt.
Close one eye, then the other, while keeping the pencil still.
It appears to jump. Each eye has its own stripes of input in the cortex, merged in the layers above.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.04 Sensory Systems · The lateral geniculate nucleus and the visual cortex

words.meaning: Lateral geniculate nucleus, the visual relay in the thalamus.
Primary visual cortex at the back of the brain, the first cortical stage of vision.
A cell firing most for an edge at one particular angle.
A stripe of cortex driven mainly by one eye.

paras: The optic nerve ends in the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus. It has six layers. Each layer receives one eye only, and the cells there respond much as retinal cells do, with a centre and an opposite surround.

In the primary visual cortex the picture changes. Cells respond best to edges at one angle, many only to motion in one direction, and most above the input layer combine the two eyes. A map of the visual field covers the whole area.

The centre of gaze takes far more cortex than the edge of vision, because cortex is the same thickness everywhere and the fovea has the most receptors. Beyond V1 lie more than 30 further visual areas, richly linked to each other.

items: Four upper layers
Small cells that receive midget ganglion cells: fine detail and colour.
Two lower layers
Large cells that receive parasol ganglion cells: motion and change.
One eye per layer
Layers alternate between the two eyes. The left thalamus sees the right half of the world.
Orientation
Cells prefer edges at one angle. This was found by chance, when the edge of a projector slide made a cell fire.
Direction
Many cells fire for movement one way and stay quiet for the reverse.
Spatial frequency
Cells prefer stripes of a certain fineness, neither too coarse nor too fine.
Two eyes
Above the input layer, most cells respond to both eyes, which prepares depth.
Simple cells
Separate zones for light and for dark, side by side.
Complex cells
Larger fields that respond to light and dark edges anywhere inside them.
Eye stripes
Input from each eye forms alternating stripes, finer than the ridges of a fingerprint.
Orientation pinwheels
Optical imaging shows preferred angles swirling around central points, messier than early tidy models.
Mirror maps
Where one visual area meets the next, the map of the visual field reverses like a mirror.
blocks.end: A good model is a tool, not a belief. Several neat diagrams of V1 were dropped once better images arrived.

blocks.h: A few of the higher areas
items: V2
Receptive fields about three times larger than in V1, organised in thick, thin and pale stripes.
V4
Large, complex fields that change with attention and eye movements. Not only a colour area.
MT
Almost every cell is tuned to direction of motion. Fed mainly by the parasol system.
blocks.end: Each area handles several kinds of information. The idea of one area per feature has not held up.

blocks.text: Early researchers shone diffuse light into the eye and found no response in the visual cortex. The cells were there all along; they simply ignore even light and wait for an edge.

entries.title: ON and OFF Channels
entries.what: The retina splits its output into two parallel channels: ON cells signal places that become brighter than their background, OFF cells signal places that become darker.
entries.gives: Seeing dark print on a light page uses the OFF system, seeing a bright star the ON system. Splitting the two lets the eye report both quickly and with excitation.
entries.pic: A bright spot and a dark spot side by side, each feeding its own line.

steps.t: Look at a page of dark text on a white background.
The letters are darker than their surround. OFF cells carry most of this signal.
Look at a white light on a dark wall at night.
Now ON cells carry the signal. Each channel has its own cells, its own wiring and its own receptor chemistry.
Stare at a bright window for 20 seconds, then look at a plain wall.
A dark afterimage appears. Adapted cells answer the plain wall with the opposite signal.

entries.safety: Never look at the sun or a bright lamp, and stop if your eyes strain or water.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.04 Sensory Systems · The ON and OFF channels

words.meaning: A cell excited when its receptive field becomes brighter than the background.
A cell excited when its receptive field becomes darker than the background.
The glutamate receptor of ON bipolar cells. It inverts the receptor signal and is found almost only in the retina.

blocks.h: Two channels from the first synapse
paras: Receptors release glutamate in the dark and less in light. The bipolar cells that listen to them come in two kinds. OFF bipolars follow the receptor signal. ON bipolars use a special receptor, mGluR6, which inverts it, so they are excited by light.

From there the two channels stay apart. ON and OFF ganglion cells branch in separate sublayers of the retina, and each type tiles the retina evenly on its own, ignoring the other. They are two complete, overlapping systems.
A drug called APB fills the ON receptor and freezes it. It allowed researchers to switch off the ON channel alone, for about 15 minutes, and watch what the rest of the visual system could still do.

blocks.h: What happens when ON is blocked
items: ON-centre cells in the thalamus stop responding to light. OFF-centre cells carry on as before.
OFF cells keep their full surround, so centre and surround do not come from the ON-OFF interplay.
Cortical cells lose their response to light edges but keep their tuning to angle, direction and stripe width.
In a task, light spots are found barely above chance and slowly; dark spots are found as quickly as ever.
After the drug washes out, every response returns.
blocks.end: The tuning of cortical cells is built by circuits in the cortex itself, not by mixing ON and OFF inputs.

items: One rod bipolar
Rods have only an ON-type bipolar cell. Block it and night vision fails for both light and dark spots.
A shared route
A special amacrine cell passes the rod signal into the cone ON and OFF pathways, so rods and cones share ganglion cells.
Bigger fields at night
In the dark, receptive fields widen and colour responses vanish. A red rose looks black by moonlight.
blocks.end: People with congenital night blindness often lack the ON channel and may be limited to daytime driving.

items: Light on dark
A predator lit from above looks bright to a fish below. ON cells catch it fast.
Dark on light
A bird against the sky looks dark. So does print on paper. OFF cells catch these.
Speed
Both changes are signalled by an increase in firing, which is faster than waiting for a drop.

blocks.text: Every quick eye movement wipes the retina clean. Transmitter is cleared so fast that the old image is gone within a fraction of a second, ready for the next fixation.

entries.title: Fine Detail and Fast Change
entries.what: Two parallel systems run from retina to cortex. The midget system carries fine detail, texture, colour and fine depth. The parasol system carries fast flicker and fast, faint motion.
entries.gives: It explains why camouflage fails the moment an animal moves, and why the edge of vision is good at catching movement but poor at reading.
entries.pic: A fine checkerboard on one side, a sweeping arc of motion on the other.

steps.t: Look straight ahead and hold a page of small print out to one side.
You see that something is there but cannot read it. Midget cells, needed for detail, thin out away from the centre.
Keep your gaze ahead and wiggle the page.
The movement jumps out at once. Parasol cells are relatively common in the periphery.
Look at a fluorescent tube or old screen out of the corner of your eye.
Flicker is often easier to see off-centre, where the parasol system carries more weight.

entries.safety: Never look at the sun or a bright lamp, and stop if your eyes strain or water.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.04 Sensory Systems · The midget and parasol systems

words.meaning: The small-cell layers of the thalamus that relay the midget system.
The large-cell layers of the thalamus that relay the parasol system.
Depth seen from the small difference between the two eyes' images.
How fine a pattern is: many narrow stripes per degree is high, a few wide ones is low.

paras: Midget ganglion cells have small fields and a sustained response. Parasol cells have fields about three times wider and fire a brief burst. In the fovea midget cells outnumber parasol cells eight to one; in the periphery the two are about equal.

To learn what each system does, small areas of either the small-cell or the large-cell layers of the thalamus were silenced in monkeys. The animals were then tested on many visual tasks, with targets placed in the affected or the healthy part of the visual field.

The result is a clear division of labour. Neither system is enough alone, and many tasks use both. The two exist because one cell cannot be both sustained and brief, or both finely detailed and highly sensitive.

blocks.h: Lost when the small-cell layers are silenced
items: Colour
Colour discrimination disappears completely.
Fine detail
Sensitivity to fine stripes drops sharply.
Texture
A patch of differently tilted lines can no longer be picked out.
Pattern
Small differences between checkerboards are missed.
Fine depth
Small differences between the two eyes' images are no longer seen as depth.
Shape
Fine form suffers; coarse form survives.

blocks.h: Lost when the large-cell layers are silenced
items: Fast flicker
Rapid flicker is badly affected.
Fast motion
Faint, fast-moving dots are much harder to see.
Nothing else much
Colour, detail and depth stay normal.
Brightness
Telling two greys apart survives either loss, in daylight and at night.
Coarse form and depth
Large shapes and large depth differences use both systems.
Night vision
Rods feed both systems, not only the parasol system as once claimed.
MT
Silenced when the parasol layers are blocked. It leads on to the parietal lobe and motion.
V4
Reduced by blocking either system. Its input is mixed, not purely midget.
V1
Some cells receive one system, others receive both.

blocks.text: A random-dot stereogram shows no shape to either eye alone. Only when the brain compares the two images does a square float above the background.

entries.title: Adaptation and Colour
entries.what: Three cone types with overlapping sensitivity code colour by their ratio, and the retina adapts to light levels that differ ten-billion-fold by signalling contrast instead of absolute light.
entries.gives: It explains colour blindness, afterimages, why white is a mixture, and how a page looks white both indoors and in sunshine.
entries.pic: A prism splitting a beam into bands, with the colour circle beside it.

steps.t: Find a strongly coloured object, such as a red cup, on a plain white wall.
Stare at its centre for 30 seconds without moving your eyes.
Move your gaze to the white wall.
A green ghost appears. Afterimages take the opposite colour across the colour circle.
Repeat with one eye closed, then switch eyes when you look at the wall.
The other eye sees no afterimage. Adaptation happens in the retina, not higher up.

entries.safety: Never look at the sun or a bright lamp, and stop if your eyes strain or water.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.04 Sensory Systems · Adaptation and colour

words.meaning: Colour vision based on three cone types, with colour read from their relative activity.
Red against green and blue against yellow: pairs that cancel and never mix into one hue.
How much a target differs from its background, relative to the overall light level.
Two colours of equal brightness, so they differ only in hue.

paras: Newton passed sunlight through a prism and found a band of colours. A second prism could not split any single colour further. White light, then, is a mixture of all visible wavelengths, not a pure colour.

The eye uses three cone types, most sensitive to short, medium and long wavelengths. Each responds broadly; colour is read from how strongly each type is driven relative to the others. Three receptors are enough to code thousands of hues.

Cells after the cones work in opposing pairs: red against green, blue against yellow, light against dark. This is why there is a yellowish green but never a reddish green, and why afterimages appear in the opposite colour.

items: Hue
Which colour it is: red, green, blue. Arranged around the colour circle.
Saturation
How vivid it is, from grey at the centre of the circle to pure colour at the rim.
Brightness
How light or dark it is, the third axis of the colour solid.
blocks.end: Colour and brightness are experiences. Wavelength and light intensity are their physical causes.

blocks.h: When a cone type is missing
items: Protan
The long-wavelength (red) cones are missing or altered.
Deutan
The medium-wavelength (green) cones are missing or altered.
Tritan
The short-wavelength (blue) cones are missing. Rare.
Who
About 8% of men of European descent, fewer in other groups, and about ten times fewer women.
Plate tests
A number hidden in coloured dots is invisible to some people with colour deficiency.
Arrangement tests
Coloured caps are put in order of hue; the pattern of errors shows the type.

blocks.h: Seeing at noon and at dusk
items: Light levels across a day span about ten billion to one.
The pupil adjusts by only about sixteen to one, so it contributes little.
Most adjustment happens in the receptors, as their pigment is used up in bright light and restored in the dark.
About 95% of ganglion cells report contrast, the difference from the background, rather than absolute light.
So a white page sends a similar signal indoors and outdoors.
blocks.end: Hold an image perfectly still on the retina and it fades within a minute. Vision depends on change.

items: Midget system
Silencing it removes colour vision entirely.
Cardinal axes
Thalamus cells cluster on red-green and blue-yellow. In-between hues are computed in the cortex.
Many areas
Damage to V4 leaves only small colour deficits. Colour is handled across several areas.

blocks.text: Blue cones are nearly absent from the very centre of the fovea. Fine blue text on black is harder to read than the same text in red or green.

entries.title: Depth Perception
entries.what: The retina is flat, so the brain rebuilds depth from several cues: the difference between the two eyes, relative motion, shading, perspective, size and overlap.
entries.gives: Depth guides every reach, step and catch. Knowing the cues explains why people without stereo vision can still drive, and why threading a needle is hard with one eye.
entries.pic: Two eyes converging on a near point, with a far point behind in bronze.

steps.t: Hold a needle and thread, or a pen and its cap, in front of you.
Put the cap on the pen with both eyes open, then with one eye closed.
With one eye it is clumsy. Stereo vision is strongest within about three metres.
Hold a thumb at arm's length and move your head from side to side.
The thumb sweeps across the background faster than distant objects. This motion parallax works at any distance.
Look at a photograph of a long road.
Converging edges and shrinking objects give depth from perspective, even on a flat page.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.04 Sensory Systems · Depth perception

words.meaning: The small difference between where an object lands on the two retinas.
Near objects sweeping across the retina faster than far ones when you or they move.
Reduced vision in one eye from poor use in early childhood, often called lazy eye.
Eyes that do not point at the same place: turned in or out.

blocks.h: Three dimensions from two flat images
paras: Because the eyes sit apart, each sees a slightly different view. Cells in the visual cortex compare the two and respond to particular differences: some to objects at the point of focus, some nearer, some farther.

A handful of broadly tuned disparity channels, perhaps four to six, are enough to compute fine depth, much as three cone types are enough for colour. A shift of a single pixel on a screen can be seen as depth.

Stereo vision is only one route. Motion parallax, shading, perspective and overlap all add depth. When cues agree, depth is seen faster and more surely; when they conflict, the picture becomes unstable.

items: Stereopsis
Disparity between the two eyes. Best at close range.
Motion parallax
Relative motion as you move. Works at long distances.
Shading
Light has come from above for millions of years. A disc lit on top looks like a bump.
Perspective
Parallel lines converge and objects shrink with distance.
Overlap
An object that hides part of another is nearer.
Eye muscles
Focusing and turning the eyes inward give a rough sense of distance.

blocks.h: When the two eyes never learned to work together
items: Who
About 5 to 10% of people lack stereo vision, often after a squint or lazy eye in childhood.
Timing
Correcting the eyes after about age eight to ten does not restore stereo vision. Early treatment matters.
Living with it
Other cues still give depth. Most stereo-blind people drive and play sports.
Single cells in V1 are tuned to near, far or zero disparity.
Removing V4 or MT does not remove stereo vision, only slows it by tens of milliseconds.
Removing MT does impair depth from motion parallax.
Brain scans show depth cues activating many visual areas, some shared and some specific to one cue.
Monkeys judge depth fastest and most accurately when stereo, parallax and shading are combined.
blocks.end: Depth is computed across many areas at once, and speed matters as much as accuracy.

items: Hammerhead shark
Eyes far apart magnify disparity.
Aerial photographs
Cameras set wide apart revealed camouflaged objects rising from the ground.
Stereoscope
A nineteenth-century viewer that shows each eye its own photograph, producing vivid depth.

blocks.text: Show one eye the first half of a word and the other eye the second half, and most people with stereo vision read the whole word. People who cannot fuse the two usually lack stereo vision.

entries.title: Form Perception
entries.what: Recognising shapes depends on whole patterns, not on adding up pieces. The brain uses coarse and fine detail, grouping rules and broadly tuned cells spread over many areas.
entries.gives: It explains why a face is still recognisable in a sketch of dots, why upside-down faces are hard, and why pixelating a face hides who it is.
entries.pic: A dotted circle seen as a whole circle, with one section in bronze.

steps.t: Find a photograph of a well-known face.
Look at it with your eyes half closed, so it blurs.
You still know who it is. Coarse detail carries much of identity.
Turn the photograph upside down.
Recognition becomes slow and uncertain. The face system is tuned to upright faces.
Write the same word in three different handwritings and sizes.
You read each instantly. Recognition holds across size, style and position.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.04 Sensory Systems · Form perception

words.meaning: The view that a whole is perceived differently from the sum of its parts.
An edge you see where no edge is drawn, completed by the brain.
Seeing an object as the same despite changes in size, angle or light.

blocks.h: More than the sum of its parts
paras: Around 1900, one school held that perception is a sum of basic sensations, like bricks in a wall. The list of elements grew past 40,000 and the idea collapsed. The Gestalt school replied that we see wholes first: a car behind railings is still a car.

Three brain theories followed. Shapes are built from line segments; the cortex holds a picture that the mind reads; or the visual system analyses scenes into stripes of different fineness. None explains everything, but the third has the most support.
In higher areas, single cells respond best to some shapes but also to many others. A shape is coded by the pattern across tens of thousands of broadly tuned cells, not by one cell per object.

items: Proximity
Items close together are seen as a group.
Similarity
Items alike in colour or shape group together.
Common motion
Items moving together belong together.
Closure
Gaps are filled so outlines look complete.
Figure and ground
One region is seen as object, the other as background, and they can flip.
Continuity
Smooth lines are followed through crossings.

blocks.h: Why a picture in the cortex cannot be the answer
items: Distortion
The centre of gaze takes far more cortex, so the cortical copy of a shape is badly distorted.
Split
A circle on the midline lands in two separate halves of the brain, yet looks round.
Equal arrows
Two equal arrows produce very unequal activity, yet look equal.
Dot portraits
Faces drawn only with dots are easily recognised, even blurred. Coarse detail carries identity.
Pixelation
Blocky pixels add sharp false edges that mask the coarse pattern, so the face is hidden.
Separate channels
Staring at stripes of one fineness lowers sensitivity to that fineness only.
V1 cells respond to orientation and fineness of pattern.
Some V2 cells respond to illusory edges, where no line is drawn.
Without V4, monkeys struggle to match shapes that are resized, partly hidden or faint.
V4 also helps select a subtle target instead of the most eye-catching one.
Inferotemporal cortex holds cells tuned to complex shapes and faces.
blocks.end: How the brain settles an ambiguous figure, such as a vase that is also two faces, is still unknown.

blocks.text: Around 1430, European paintings jumped to near-photographic realism. One argument holds that artists used lenses to project scenes onto the canvas; a clue is the number of left-handed sitters, as projected images are reversed.

entries.title: Illusions and Visual Prostheses
entries.what: Illusions reveal the rules the visual system uses, and those same rules shape how a prosthesis in the visual cortex has to be designed to restore some sight.
entries.gives: Illusions show that seeing is an active construction. A visual prosthesis is one of the main hopes for the more than 40 million blind people worldwide.
entries.pic: A grid with grey spots at the crossings, beside a grid of electrode dots.

steps.t: Draw a grid of thick black squares with white lines between them, or find a Hermann grid online.
Look at the grid without fixing on one crossing.
Grey spots flicker at the crossings you are not looking at. The spot vanishes wherever you look directly.
Look at two equal grey squares, one on a dark and one on a light background.
The square on dark looks lighter. The visual system compares neighbours and judges brightness by contrast.

entries.safety: Never look at the sun or a bright lamp, and stop if your eyes strain or water.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.04 Sensory Systems · Illusions and visual prosthesis

words.meaning: A small spot of light seen when the visual cortex is stimulated electrically.
After watching steady motion, still things appear to drift the other way.
Showing a different image to each eye.

paras: An illusion is not a fault. It shows a rule the visual system relies on, applied where it does not fit. Testing when an illusion appears and disappears tells us at which stage of the system it arises.

Two tests are especially useful. If an illusion still works when each part is shown to a different eye, it arises in the cortex, after the eyes combine. If it vanishes when the colours are made equally bright, it depends on brightness channels.

The same findings guide the design of visual prostheses. A good device has to place electrodes the way the cortex devotes space, with many more near the centre of gaze, and send signals mainly at edges, as cortical cells do.

items: Hermann grid
Grey spots at crossings. The textbook retinal explanation fails many tests; cortical cells are more likely.
Brightness contrast
Equal greys look different on different backgrounds. Brightness is judged locally.
Cafe wall
Offset tiles with grey mortar make parallel rows look tilted.
Arrow lengths
Fins on a line change how long it looks. It survives one part per eye, so it is cortical.
Figure and ground
A vase or two faces; an old woman or a young one. The brain flips between readings.
Waterfall
After watching downward motion, still rocks seem to rise. Motion cells fatigue.
Afterimages
Fixate a pattern and look away; a reversed image appears. Switching eyes removes it.
Colour ghosts
A moving magenta spot leaves a green trail, the opposite colour.
Brightness masking
A bright flash wipes out a dimmer one shown just before it, because bright signals travel faster.
The retina and thalamus degenerate in many forms of blindness, so the visual cortex is a promising site.
A small current in the visual cortex produces a phosphene, a faint star-like spot.
Spacing electrodes evenly distorts shapes into a butterfly. Spacing them like the cortex keeps shapes true.
A camera feeds software that activates electrodes only where edges fall, ignoring flat areas.
In simulations, shapes and moving words become readable with a few hundred well-placed electrodes.
blocks.end: Long-term tissue reaction around electrodes remains a central problem.

blind people worldwide

blocks.text: Many illusions disappear when the two colours involved are set to equal brightness. That points to the brightness channels, not the colour channels, as their source.

entries.title: Eye Movements: The Brainstem and Colliculus
entries.what: Six muscles move each eye. Brainstem neurons set eye position by their firing rate, and the superior colliculus holds a map that turns a place in the visual field into a saccade of the right size and direction.
entries.gives: We make about three quick eye movements every second, over 150,000 a day, each one a decision about where to look next.
entries.pic: An eye with six muscle lines, and a map with a vector arrow in bronze.

steps.t: Ask someone to look at a picture of a face while you watch their eyes.
Their eyes jump, not glide. Fixations cluster on the eyes, mouth and edges, rarely on smooth areas.
Ask them to follow your slowly moving finger.
Now the eyes glide smoothly. Pursuit needs a moving target; it cannot be done on an empty wall.
Look at a word and shake your head gently.
The word stays clear. A reflex moves the eyes against the head to keep the image steady.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.04 Sensory Systems · The neural control of visually guided eye movements 1

words.meaning: A fast jump of the eyes from one point to the next.
Slow, steady tracking of a moving object.
A layered structure on the roof of the midbrain that directs the eyes towards targets.
The eyes turning inward or outward together to look near or far.

paras: Only the fovea sees sharply, and it covers a tiny part of the scene. The eyes must jump constantly to bring targets onto it. Other movements track moving objects, keep the image steady while the head moves, and turn the eyes inward for near targets.

Each eye has six muscles, driven by three cranial nerves. The eye has no load to carry, which makes its control unusually clear. Motor neurons fire at a rate that matches eye position, add a burst to jump and fall silent to let the opposite muscle pull.

Above them, the superior colliculus works differently. A site in its map codes a movement of a fixed size and direction. Stimulate it longer and the eye makes repeated equal jumps instead of one larger jump.

items: Saccades
Fast jumps that bring a target onto the fovea. About three per second.
Smooth pursuit
Steady tracking of a moving target, such as a bird in flight.
Stabilisation
Reflexes from the balance organs keep the image still while the head moves.
Vergence
The eyes turn inward or outward together for near or far targets.
Optokinetic
Following a moving scene, with a quick reset, as from a train window.
Fixation
Holding the gaze steady on one point between movements.
Rate code
Brainstem motor neurons fire faster the further the eye turns. Burst length sets the size of a jump.
Vector code
Each site in the colliculus codes one size and direction of movement, whatever the starting point.
Same neurons
The same motor neurons drive jumps, pursuit and steady holding.

blocks.h: From seeing a target to moving towards it
items: The top layer receives direct input from the retina and maps the opposite half of the visual field.
The next layer receives input from the visual cortex.
Deeper layers fire just before a jump of a particular size and direction.
Each site's movement field lines up with its visual field, so seeing and moving share one map.
In primates, the cortex drives the deeper layers. Without V1 they stop responding to light.
blocks.end: In fish and frogs the colliculus is the main visual centre. In primates it shrank as the cortex took over.

items: 3 per second
saccades while you look around

muscles move each eye

5-6 mm

blocks.text: When people view a painting of a horse and rider, their first fixations go to the rider's eyes, then the horse's. Where we look reveals what we judge important.

entries.title: Eye Movements: Choosing Where to Look
entries.what: Two linked cortical systems drive the eyes: a rear one through the superior colliculus and a front one through the frontal eye fields. Together with inhibitory circuits they pick one target out of many.
entries.gives: Each glance involves a hidden decision: what is there, what to look at, what to ignore and when to move. These circuits show how the brain makes a choice.
entries.pic: Two pathways, rear and front, converging on one eye, with a single chosen target in bronze.

steps.t: Sit facing a friend and hold up both hands, one on each side of their head.
Wiggle one finger and ask them to look at it as fast as they can.
They pick it at once. Selecting one target is quick when it appears alone.
Now wiggle both fingers at the same moment.
They hesitate and choose one side. The brain must suppress the other target to avoid looking in between.
Wiggle one finger slightly before the other.
They almost always look at the first. A head start of a few tens of milliseconds decides the choice.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.04 Sensory Systems · The neural control of visually guided eye movements 2

words.meaning: An area of the frontal lobe that plans eye movements and connects directly to the brainstem.
A very fast eye movement, about 100 ms, that depends on the superior colliculus.
The main inhibitory transmitter of the brain.

paras: Several areas can trigger eye movements: V1, V2, the parietal area LIP, the frontal eye fields and the medial eye fields. The rear areas work through the superior colliculus. The frontal areas also reach the brainstem directly.

Removing the colliculus alone or the frontal eye fields alone leaves eye movements largely intact. Removing both stops voluntary jumps completely, although the animal still sees and reaches accurately. The two routes are the essential pathways.

Choosing needs inhibition. Stimulate two colliculus sites at once and the eye lands halfway between them. With two real targets, it picks one. Inhibitory circuits, including the basal ganglia, let only one target through.

items: Rear system
V1, V2 and LIP act through the colliculus. Without it, stimulating them no longer moves the eyes.
Front system
Frontal and medial eye fields still work without the colliculus, through direct brainstem links.
Express saccades
Very fast jumps, about 100 ms, need the colliculus. They vanish on the side where it is lost.

blocks.h: What has to happen in about 200 ms
items: Identify
Find the possible targets in the scene.
Select
Decide which one to look at.
Suppress
Decide which not to look at, so the eye does not land between them.
Locate
Turn the chosen place into a movement vector.
Time
Decide when to move, leaving time to analyse what is seen.
Sequence
Link 20 to 30 jumps to understand a whole scene.
Muscimol increases GABA inhibition. In the colliculus it stops movements to one part of the field.
Bicuculline blocks GABA inhibition. In the colliculus it causes repeated, unwanted jumps.
In the frontal eye fields, blocking inhibition makes jumps to one area almost irresistible.
In V1, both drugs disturb the analysis of the image itself.
In LIP, neither drug changes eye movements much.
blocks.end: The effects wash out within a day, which lets each area be tested in the same animal.

items: Frontal eye fields
Planning two quick successive jumps suffers, and choice is biased to the healthy side for years.
Medial eye fields
Small effects, with full recovery within about four months. They help decide how long to look.
Colliculus
Express saccades disappear for good; ordinary jumps become slower.

blocks.text: The eyes move rapidly during dreaming sleep in many animals. One idea is practical: regular movement keeps the eyeball round and the cornea smooth.

entries.title: Motion Perception and Pursuit
entries.what: Cells in V1 and especially in area MT respond to particular directions and speeds of motion. Motion reveals hidden shapes and drives the eyes to track moving objects.
entries.gives: Motion breaks camouflage, tells us how others move, and keeps the image steady while we travel. Films and screens work only because the brain sees apparent motion.
entries.pic: A wheel with spokes, one spoke in bronze, and a curved arrow.

steps.t: Watch a video of a car or carriage wheel accelerating.
At some speed the wheel seems to turn backwards. Each frame shows the nearest spoke slightly behind its earlier place.
Stare at a waterfall or scrolling text for 30 seconds, then look at a still wall.
The wall seems to drift the other way. Cells tuned to the first direction have tired.
Look out of a moving train window.
Your eyes follow the scene, then flick back, again and again. This is the optokinetic reflex.

entries.safety: Never look at the sun or a bright lamp, and stop if your eyes strain or water.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.04 Sensory Systems · Motion perception and pursuit eye movements

words.meaning: A cell firing for motion in one direction and not the reverse.
Seeing smooth movement from a sequence of still images, as in film.
Slow tracking of a moving scene followed by a quick reset, repeated.
An area beyond MT with very large fields, tuned to straight, circular and expanding motion.

paras: Most cells in the primary visual cortex respond to motion in one direction more than the opposite. In area MT nearly every cell does, and motion the wrong way actively inhibits it. MST, beyond MT, has fields tens of degrees wide that remain tightly tuned.

Direction tuning is built by lopsided inhibition. In the rabbit retina, blocking an inhibitory transmitter removes it, and it returns when the drug washes out. The same principle is thought to work in the cortex.
Without MT, monkeys struggle to see moving dots and flicker, even colour flicker. Without V4 they do not. Motion and flicker depend on the parasol route that runs through MT.

items: Straight
An object crossing the field.
Circular
A spinning wheel.
Expanding
The scene streaming outward as you drive forward; contracting as you reverse.
blocks.end: Most MST cells respond to two or three of these. Perception comes from groups of cells, not single detectors.

items: Breaking camouflage
A still insect on bark is invisible until it moves.
Points of light
A dozen lights on a person's joints look random when still, and like a walking person when moving.
Apparent motion
Two dots flashing in turn look like one dot jumping.
Global rules
Many separate ambiguous displays all flip direction together, as if one decision rules them.
Backward wheels
Film shows fast wheels turning the wrong way. This never happens in continuous daylight.
Flicker
Early films at 16 frames per second flickered. Showing each frame three times removed it.
A moving scene drives slow tracking of the eyes.
A quick jump resets them, and the cycle repeats.
Special retinal cells tuned to slow motion feed a dedicated pathway.
Their three preferred directions match the three canals of the balance organ.
The signal passes through the cerebellum to the eye-muscle nuclei.
blocks.end: If one eye is held still, the other eye tracks faster and faster, because the feedback loop is broken.

items: Ring after disc
A ring shown about 60-100 ms after a disc hides it, even when each goes to a different eye. This arises in the cortex.
Bright after dim
A bright disc wipes out a dimmer one shown just before. It fails across the eyes, so it arises in the retina.
Why
Brighter signals travel faster and overtake the dimmer signal on the way to the brain.

blocks.text: From a few moving lights on the joints of two dancers in the dark, viewers can tell which dancer is the man and which the woman.

entries.title: Vision: The Whole System
entries.what: A summary of the visual system from eye to eye movements: parallel channels from the retina, feature analysis in the cortex, many specialised but overlapping areas, and two routes that point the eyes.
entries.gives: Seeing the whole system at once shows its logic: split the signal early, analyse it in parallel, and combine the results to guide action.
entries.pic: A chain of boxes from eye to cortex and back to the eye muscles.

steps.t: Sit in a room with a window and a patterned object in view.
Look from the window to the object and back.
Your pupils, receptors and contrast coding adjust within seconds. A white page stays white in both light levels.
Look at the patterned object and name its colour, shape and distance.
Parallel channels carried each quality, and the cortex combined them in under a fifth of a second.
Count how often your eyes jump while you look around the room for ten seconds.
About 30 jumps, each one chosen by the eye-movement circuits.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.04 Sensory Systems · Review: the visual and oculomotor systems

words.meaning: Several channels handling different aspects of the same input at the same time.
The shift of functions from older brainstem centres to the cortex over evolution.
The much larger area of cortex given to the centre of gaze than to the periphery.

blocks.h: The visual system in one view
paras: The eye splits its output early. ON and OFF cells report light and dark changes; midget and parasol cells report detail and colour versus motion and flicker. Each eye's signals go to separate layers of the thalamus and meet in the visual cortex.

The cortex analyses features: orientation, direction, fineness, colour and depth. More than 30 areas with over 300 connections share the work. No area has a single job, but damage reveals strong leanings: MT for motion and flicker, V4 for choosing subtle targets.

Throughout, the system codes contrast rather than absolute light, because cells can fire at most a few hundred times a second while light varies ten-billion-fold. And it moves the eyes about three times a second to keep the sharp fovea on what matters.

rows: V4 and temporal lobe: form and objects

items: Contrast, not light
Most cells report differences from the background.
Parallel channels
ON and OFF, midget and parasol, each with its own range.
Feature analysis
V1 breaks the image into edges, directions and stripe widths.
Distributed areas
Colour, form and depth are handled across many areas.
Maps
Areas keep a map of the visual field, with the centre greatly enlarged.
Action
Vision exists to guide behaviour, starting with where to look.
Midget system
Colour, fine detail, texture and fine depth are lost.
MT
Motion and flicker suffer badly; depth from stereo survives.
V4
Basic tasks recover, but picking subtle targets and learning new shapes stay hard.

entries.title: Sound and the Ear
entries.what: Sound is a pressure wave in air. The outer ear collects it and shapes it, the middle ear passes it from air into fluid, and the inner ear sorts it by frequency.
entries.gives: Understanding the ear explains decibels, why some hearing losses can be repaired by surgery, and how the shape of your ear helps you hear height.
entries.pic: An outer ear, three small bones and a coiled cochlea in bronze.

steps.t: Sit somewhere quiet with your eyes closed and ask a friend to jingle keys around your head.
Point to where the sound comes from, including high and low positions.
You point well. The folds of the outer ear filter sound differently from each height.
Swallow or yawn while gently pinching your nose, as on a plane.
Your ears pop. A small tube equalises air pressure on both sides of the eardrum.
Hum with your ears blocked by your fingers.
The hum gets louder. Sound reaches the inner ear through the bones of the skull too.

entries.safety: Keep any test sound at a comfortable level, and stop at once if your ears ring or hurt.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.04 Sensory Systems · Sound, external, middle and inner ears

words.meaning: A logarithmic scale of sound pressure. Every 20 dB is a tenfold rise in pressure.
The three small bones of the middle ear: hammer, anvil and stirrup.
The quality that makes a piano and a guitar sound different on the same note.
Loss caused by a problem in the outer or middle ear, before the cochlea.

paras: Sound is mechanical vibration carried through air, water or solids. A loudspeaker pushes and pulls the air, making tiny pressure swings above and below normal air pressure. There is no sound in a vacuum.

Getting sound from air into the fluid of the inner ear is hard: about 99.5% of sound bounces off a water surface. The middle ear solves this. A large eardrum collects force onto a small footplate, and the three bones add leverage, raising the pressure.
Without the eardrum and bones, hearing drops by about 40 dB. That is a serious loss, but not deafness, and surgery or a hearing aid can often restore it.

items: Frequency
Vibrations per second, in hertz. Young humans hear about 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
Level
Measured in decibels. 0 dB is roughly the faintest audible 1 kHz tone.
Pitch
Where a sound sits on a musical scale, mainly set by its fundamental frequency.
Harmonics
Instruments vibrate at the fundamental and at its multiples.
Timbre
The pattern of harmonics, which makes each instrument and voice distinct.
Smallest changes
About 1 dB in level and about 2 Hz at 1,000 Hz in frequency.
Outer ear
The visible ear and a 3 cm canal ending at the eardrum, which is as thin as plastic wrap.
Middle ear
An air-filled space with the three smallest bones of the body. The stirrup presses on the oval window.
Inner ear
The cochlea, the size of an aspirin tablet, in the hardest bone of the skull. The balance canals sit beside it.
0 dB
faintest sound young ears detect
60 dB
normal conversation
85 dB
level where hearing protection is advised over a working day
100 dB
chainsaw or leaf blower
120 dB
pain begins; damage after brief exposure
gunshot or jet engine close by
Sound reflects off the folds of the outer ear before entering the canal.
Reflections cancel the direct sound at certain frequencies, cutting sharp notches in the spectrum.
The notches move with the height of the sound source.
In one study, moulds placed in the ears ruined people's judgement of height but not of left and right.
After a few weeks wearing them, people learned their new ears and judged height well again.
blocks.end: Left and right come from comparing the two ears. Height comes from the shape of each ear.

blocks.text: The decibel reference was set in the 1930s by testing the hearing of a few dozen people at a county fair. Young listeners often hear slightly better, so values below 0 dB are possible.

entries.title: Hair Cells and the Cochlear Amplifier
entries.what: Hair cells turn vibration into electrical signals. Inner hair cells report to the brain; outer hair cells change length with each vibration and amplify the motion of the cochlea.
entries.gives: Hair cells do not regrow in mammals, so their loss is the main cause of permanent hearing loss. Their activity even produces faint sounds that are used to screen newborns.
entries.pic: A hair cell with its stepped bundle, one bundle tilted in bronze.

steps.t: Sit in a very quiet room for two minutes.
Listen closely to the silence.
Many people notice a faint hum or ring. Some ears also give out a faint sound, measurable with a microphone.
Hum a low note, then a high note, with a hand on your throat and the other on your head.
Low notes vibrate the far end of the cochlea; high notes the near end. Each spot along it has its own best frequency.

entries.safety: Keep any test sound at a comfortable level, and stop at once if your ears ring or hurt.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.04 Sensory Systems · Hair cells

words.meaning: The flexible strip running along the cochlea on which the hair cells sit.
The stiff rods on top of a hair cell. Bending them opens channels.
The motor protein that makes outer hair cells change length.
A faint sound produced by the inner ear, recorded in the ear canal.

blocks.h: A wave along a coiled strip
paras: Inside the cochlea, sound sets up a travelling wave along the basilar membrane. The base is narrow and stiff and responds to high pitches; the far end is wide and heavy and responds to low pitches. The coil only saves space.

The first measurements were made in cadaver ears at very loud levels and showed broad tuning. In living ears, measured with lasers, each point is far more sharply tuned at quiet levels. Something alive was sharpening the response.

That something is the outer hair cell. It shortens and lengthens in time with the sound, adding force at the right moment. This cochlear amplifier adds roughly 40 to 60 dB of sensitivity and sharpens tuning.

items: Sound moves the basilar membrane and bends the bundle of stereocilia on each hair cell.
Fine tip links pull open channels at the tops of the stereocilia.
Potassium flows in from the surrounding fluid and the cell becomes charged.
Inner hair cells release glutamate onto auditory nerve fibres.
Outer hair cells change length and push the membrane, amplifying the motion.
blocks.end: The hairs are stiff rods packed with actin. They pivot at the base like poles in a storm.

items: Inner hair cells
One row, about 3,500 per ear. About 95% of nerve fibres carrying sound to the brain contact them.
Outer hair cells
Three rows, about 12,000 per ear. Few fibres report from them; they act as the amplifier.
Teamwork
Without outer hair cells, sensitivity drops 40 to 60 dB and tuning becomes broad.

blocks.h: What hair cells mean for health
items: No regrowth
Mammals never replace lost hair cells. Supporting cells form scars.
Birds regrow
Birds replace hair cells within weeks, which drives research into repair.
Causes of loss
Loud noise, some antibiotics, meningitis and ageing.
Newborn screening
A click in the ear canal evokes an echo from healthy outer hair cells.
Tinnitus
Ringing with no sound in the ear. It arises in the brain, like a phantom limb.
No cancer
Inner ear cells do not divide, so tumours do not arise from them.

blocks.text: Isolated outer hair cells, driven by an electrical copy of music, visibly stretch and shrink in time with it. No other cell in the body moves like this at sound frequencies.

entries.title: The Auditory Nerve and Pitch
entries.what: About 30,000 nerve fibres carry sound from each ear. Each is tuned to a best frequency set by its place in the cochlea, and at low frequencies fibres also fire in step with the sound wave.
entries.gives: These two codes, place and timing, explain how finely we tell pitches apart, why octaves sound pure, and why a damaged ear hears but cannot understand.
entries.pic: A V-shaped tuning curve with its tip marked in bronze.

steps.t: Use a tone generator app at a comfortable, low volume.
Play 1,000 Hz, then 1,005 Hz, then 1,002 Hz.
Most people hear the difference down to a few hertz. That is roughly the step from one inner hair cell to its neighbour.
Play 440 Hz together with 880 Hz, then 440 Hz with 890 Hz.
The first pair blends into one pure sound; the second beats roughly. Octave partners share timing patterns in the nerve.

entries.safety: Keep any test sound at a comfortable level, and stop at once if your ears ring or hurt.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.04 Sensory Systems · Auditory nerve; psychophysics of frequency resolution

words.meaning: The frequency a nerve fibre responds to at the lowest sound level.
Spikes timed to the same point in each cycle of a sound wave.
An orderly map of frequency, from low to high, kept through the hearing pathway.
A doubling of frequency, such as 440 Hz to 880 Hz.

paras: Each nerve fibre connects to one inner hair cell at one place along the cochlea. At quiet levels it fires only near its best frequency. Labelling single fibres showed that frequency maps onto place in an orderly, logarithmic way.
Fibres also fire in time with the sound wave, at the same point in each cycle, though not on every cycle. This timing code is strong up to about 1 kHz and fades by about 3 to 5 kHz.
High pitches are coded by place alone; low pitches by place and timing. Most music sits below about 3 kHz, where timing is available, and octave matching becomes impossible above about 5 kHz.

items: Type I
Thick, myelinated, about 95% of fibres. Up to 20 contact each inner hair cell; each fibre contacts only one.
Type II
Thin, unmyelinated, about 5%. Each branches to many outer hair cells. Their role is still unclear.
Ribbon synapse
A dense ribbon at each hair cell synapse coordinates rapid, steady release, as in the eye.
Tuning curves
V-shaped plots of the quietest sound that drives a fibre, with a sharp tip at its best frequency.
Fine discrimination
About 2 Hz at 1,000 Hz, even in untrained listeners.
Suppression
A second tone just outside the tuning curve reduces the response. This happens in the mechanics, not by inhibition.
Masking curves
Measured in people with a quiet probe tone, they match the nerve's tuning curves.
Octaves
Notes an octave apart share many spike intervals, so they blend.
Stretched octaves
Listeners set the upper note slightly sharp, because nerve recovery time shortens the shortest intervals.

Fibres need 40 to 60 dB more sound to respond.
Each fibre now responds to a broad band of frequencies.
Pitch discrimination worsens and background noise floods every channel.
A hearing aid restores loudness but cannot restore the sharp tuning.
blocks.end: This is the common complaint: "I can hear you, but I cannot understand you."

entries.title: The Cochlear Nucleus
entries.what: The cochlear nucleus is the first brain station for sound. Each incoming fibre branches to several regions, where about ten cell types split the signal into parallel streams.
entries.gives: Unlike vision, hearing passes through several brainstem stations, mainly to work out where sounds come from. The streams start here.
entries.pic: One incoming fibre branching to three differently shaped cells.

steps.t: Clap once in a small room and once in a large hall or stairwell.
You hear the sharp onset clearly in both. Some cells fire one spike at the very start of a sound.
Listen to a steady hum, such as a fridge.
Other cells fire steadily for as long as a sound lasts, some in a regular rhythm.
Cover one ear and listen to a sound off to the side, then uncover it.
Direction becomes clearer with both ears. Bushy cells send exact timing to the next station, where the ears are compared.

entries.safety: Keep any test sound at a comfortable level, and stop at once if your ears ring or hurt.

words.meaning: A cluster of nerve cells inside the brain. In the periphery the same thing is called a ganglion.
A giant nerve ending that wraps around a bushy cell; the largest synapse in the brain.
A plot of spike timing averaged over hundreds of repeats of the same sound.

paras: The auditory nerve ends in the cochlear nucleus, on the outside of the brainstem. Each fibre splits into branches that reach its ventral and dorsal parts, arranged by frequency, so the map from the cochlea is copied several times.

From here the pathway climbs through the superior olive, the inferior colliculus and the thalamus to the auditory cortex. Vision has no such chain of brainstem stations. Hearing needs them because the ear maps frequency, not space, and direction must be computed.
About ten cell types live in the nucleus, each with its own shape and firing pattern. Their outputs leave by separate tracts, forming parallel pathways much like the channels of the visual system.

items: Bushy cells
Fire much like the nerve itself. Spherical bushy cells feed the timing comparison between the ears.
Stellate cells
Fire in a regular, rhythmic pattern while the sound lasts.
Octopus cells
Dendrites spread to one side like tentacles. They fire a single spike at the onset.
Fusiform cells
In the layered dorsal part. They fire, pause about 10 ms, then fire again.
Giant synapse
The endbulb of Held wraps a bushy cell, passing timing with very little delay.
About ten types
Most have no known function yet. Each likely feeds its own pathway.

blocks.h: How cell types were matched to signals
items: Two names
Cells were named once by cell-body stains and again by whole-cell stains. Modern names combine both.
Firing patterns
Hundreds of short tones and early computers gave four main patterns: nerve-like, rhythmic, pausing and onset.
Single cells filled
Recording one cell and filling it with dye linked each pattern to a shape.
Who
People without a working auditory nerve, often after removal of nerve tumours.
How
A flat pad of 15 to 21 electrodes sits on the surface of the nucleus.
Results
Speech is rarely understood by sound alone; the device mainly helps lip-reading.

blocks.text: A Spanish anatomist's detailed drawings of these cells, made in the 1920s and 30s, waited about 30 years before they were published, and are still used today.

entries.title: Hearing Loss and Cochlear Implants
entries.what: Most permanent hearing loss comes from damaged hair cells, usually through noise, drugs, ageing, genes or disease. Hearing aids amplify; cochlear implants bypass the hair cells and stimulate the nerve.
entries.gives: Noise damage is cumulative and preventable. The cochlear implant is the most successful restoration of a human sense by medicine, used by hundreds of thousands of people.
entries.pic: An ear with a coil and an electrode array spiralling into the cochlea.

steps.t: Check the noise level of a place you visit often with a sound meter app.
Above 85 dB for long periods damages hearing. Concerts, power tools and clubs often exceed 100 dB.
Roll a foam earplug thin, insert it, and hold it while it expands.
A good fit cuts about 20 dB. Sounds are softer but still clear.
After a loud event, notice any ringing or muffled hearing.
Ringing means the inner ear was stressed. Rest your ears and protect them next time.

entries.safety: Seek a hearing test after sudden hearing loss, ear pain or lasting ringing. Never use earplugs in place of medical care.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.04 Sensory Systems · Hearing loss and cochlear implants

words.meaning: Hearing loss from the cochlea or nerve, most often lost hair cells.
A chart of the quietest sound heard at each frequency, compared with normal hearing.
Harmful to the inner ear, as some antibiotics are.
An early window when the brain learns a skill such as language most easily.

paras: Conductive loss affects the eardrum or bones and can often be repaired. Sensorineural loss affects the cochlea or nerve; in about 99% of cases the hair cells are lost. Outer hair cells and the high-frequency base of the cochlea are the most vulnerable.

A typical pattern is normal hearing to about 1 kHz and a sloping loss above. Vowels sit at low frequencies but consonants such as "s" and "t" are high, so speech becomes muffled and hard to follow, especially in noise.

In one study of a right-handed hunter, the ear nearer the gun had lost almost all its high-frequency hair cells, while the other, shielded by the head, was largely intact. The nerve fibres survived, which is what makes implants possible.

items: Noise
Gunshots and fireworks above 120 dB can damage in one exposure. Damage adds up over years.
Drugs
Some antibiotics in the aminoglycoside family kill hair cells.
Ageing
High frequencies fade with age. The mechanism is still being studied.
Genes
Inherited deafness is common enough that newborn screening is standard in many places.
Disease
Meningitis and other infections can destroy hearing.
Variation
People differ greatly in how much noise damages them.
Hearing aid
Microphone, amplifier shaped to the loss, and a tiny speaker. Excellent for conductive loss, limited when tuning is broad.
Cochlear implant
Sound is split into frequency bands and sent as pulses to about 22 electrodes along the cochlea, low pitches deep inside.
Brainstem and midbrain implants
For people without a working nerve. Results are much weaker than with cochlear implants.
At switch-on, voices sound high and cartoon-like. Within one to two months the brain adapts.
Many users understand most words without lip-reading in quiet rooms.
Noise, music and tonal languages stay hard, because implants give place but little timing information.
The device is programmed yearly in a sound booth, matching loudness and pitch for each electrode.
Children born deaf are implanted early, around 18 months, to use the critical period for language.
blocks.end: Implants are taken off for sleep, showering and swimming, so visual or vibrating alarms are used at night.

entries.title: Ear Reflexes and Descending Control
entries.what: The brain sends signals back down to the ear. Two reflexes, the olivocochlear system and the middle-ear muscles, turn hearing down to protect it, reduce masking by noise and support attention.
entries.gives: They explain why ringing ears after a loud event are a warning, why we hear speech in a noisy restaurant, and why your own voice does not deafen you.
entries.pic: An arrow going up from the ear to the brainstem, and a bronze arrow coming back down.

steps.t: Turn on a car radio at low volume on a quiet street, then on a busy road.
On the road you turn it up. Low road rumble masks the music, and your middle-ear muscles also tighten in loud noise.
Read something absorbing while music plays in the next room.
The music seems to fade. The brain can turn down the ear while you attend to vision.
Speak aloud and notice how loud your voice feels.
Middle-ear muscles contract just before and during speech, so your own voice is softened.

entries.safety: Keep any test sound at a comfortable level, and stop at once if your ears ring or hurt.

words.meaning: Nerve fibres from the superior olive in the brainstem to the hair cells of the cochlea.
The smallest muscle in the body. It pulls on the stirrup bone to damp sound.
One sound making another harder or impossible to hear.
A reflex triggered from either side that acts on both sides, like the pupils.

blocks.h: The brain turns down the ear
paras: Alongside every upward station of the hearing pathway runs a downward one. The best understood ends in the ear itself: neurons in the superior olive send fibres to the outer hair cells and to the nerve endings under the inner hair cells.

Their transmitter, acetylcholine, makes outer hair cells move less, lowering the cochlear amplifier by about 25 dB. The reflex is fast, under 5 milliseconds, and sound in either ear triggers it, much as light in one eye narrows both pupils.
A second reflex uses two tiny middle-ear muscles. They stiffen the chain of bones and cut low-pitched sound by up to about 25 dB. Both reflexes protect the ear and help us hear signals in noise.

items: Protection
With the fibres cut on one side, a loud noise damages that ear far more.
Range shift
It shifts the nerve's working range up by about 20 dB, so loud backgrounds do not saturate it.
Less masking
Noise uses up transmitter at the hair cell synapse. Turning noise down saves it for the signal.
Attention
Animals attending to a light task showed smaller ear responses to irrelevant clicks.
Band by band
Fibres are tuned and arranged by frequency, so hearing can be turned down in chosen bands.
Too fast for thought
The reflex runs through the brainstem, not the cortex.
Stapedius
Pulls on the stirrup. Controlled by the facial nerve.
Tensor tympani
Pulls on the hammer and tenses the eardrum. Controlled by the trigeminal nerve.
Low pitches
Contraction mainly cuts low frequencies, reducing masking by rumble.
blocks.end: Factory workers with a one-sided facial palsy showed temporary hearing loss only in the palsied ear after a loud shift.

blocks.h: From sound back to the ear
items: Sound excites the auditory nerve.
The nerve drives cells in the cochlear nucleus.
These cells drive olivocochlear neurons in the superior olive, on both sides.
Their fibres release acetylcholine onto outer hair cells.
The outer hair cells move less and the ear becomes less sensitive, within milliseconds.
blocks.end: Ringing after loud sound means the ear was damaged. The reflexes help, but they cannot protect against everything.

entries.title: Where Sounds Come From: Two Ears
entries.what: The brain locates sounds left and right by comparing the two ears: tiny time differences at low frequencies and level differences at high frequencies. Height and front-back come from the shape of the outer ear.
entries.gives: We can detect a shift of about one degree, which needs timing differences of about ten millionths of a second. This shows how finely the brainstem compares two inputs.
entries.pic: A head with sound reaching the near ear first and the far ear a moment later, in bronze.

steps.t: Close your eyes and ask a friend to jingle keys at different places around you.
Point to each sound, then open your eyes to check.
Most people land within about 20 degrees.
Repeat with one ear blocked.
Errors grow. Comparing two ears is the main cue for left and right.
Repeat with one ear blocked and the other ear folded forward.
The sound seems to come from everywhere. Ear shape is needed for height and for front versus back.

entries.safety: Keep any test sound at a comfortable level, and stop at once if your ears ring or hurt.

words.meaning: Interaural time difference: how much earlier a sound reaches one ear than the other.
Interaural level difference: how much louder a sound is in the nearer ear.
Direction in the horizontal plane, from left through front to right.
A cell that fires only when inputs from both sides arrive at the same moment.

paras: A sound off to one side reaches the nearer ear first. For a human head the largest delay, with the sound straight to the side, is about 0.6 thousandths of a second. The head also casts a sound shadow, so the far ear hears it more quietly.

Low frequencies bend round the head, so they give almost no level difference; the brain uses timing. High frequencies give big level differences, up to about 20 dB, but their waves are so short that ongoing timing becomes ambiguous above about 1.5 kHz.

Neither cue changes with height, and both are the same in front and behind. The folds of the outer ear fill these gaps by shaping the sound spectrum. Height judgements are much coarser than left and right.

Used at low frequencies. The smallest detectable change is about 10 microseconds.
Level difference
Used at high frequencies. The smallest detectable change is about 1 dB.
Ear shape
Gives height and front versus back. Works with one ear, but only to about 10 to 30 degrees.

Cells in the medial superior olive receive input from both ears on two separate dendrites.
They fire strongly only when both inputs arrive together.
Input fibres act as delay lines, reaching each cell along a row a little later.
Each cell therefore matches one time difference, one direction in space.
The row of cells forms a map of sound direction.
blocks.end: In birds this design is clear. In mammals, inhibition and other delay sources also play a role, and the debate continues.

blocks.k: Why timing fails at high pitch
items: Phase locking
Nerve fibres follow the wave only up to about 1 kHz. Above that, timing becomes unreliable.
Headphones
Sounds in headphones seem inside the head, because the outer ear and the room are missing.
Implants
Two cochlear implants do not keep fine timing and are not synchronised, so time cues are mostly lost.

blocks.text: A spike lasts about one thousandth of a second, yet the brain compares spikes from the two ears to within ten millionths of a second, a hundred times finer.

entries.title: Where Sounds Come From: Circuits and Rooms
entries.what: Level differences are computed by a simple balance of excitation and inhibition in the lateral superior olive. Time and level cues meet in the inferior colliculus, and the first part of a sound sets its perceived place in a room full of echoes.
entries.gives: It explains how we locate a speaker in a reverberant hall, why music halls and speech theatres are built differently, and how experience reshapes the brain's map of space.
entries.pic: A barn owl face with a small grid of map squares, one in bronze.

steps.t: Stand in a tiled bathroom or stairwell and clap once.
You hear one clap from your hands, although echoes arrive from every wall.
Ask a friend to speak while walking round you in that room, your eyes closed.
You still track them. The brain uses the first few milliseconds of each sound and suppresses later echoes.
Go outdoors to an open field and clap again.
The clap sounds dry and short. Outdoors there are no walls, so there is no reverberation.

entries.safety: Keep any test sound at a comfortable level, and stop at once if your ears ring or hurt.

words.meaning: The first-arriving sound sets the perceived direction; later echoes are suppressed.
How long sound takes to die away in a room.
An inhibitory transmitter, used here to subtract one ear from the other.
An orderly layout of neurons by the direction of the sound they respond to.

paras: In the lateral superior olive, sound in the same-side ear excites each cell. Sound in the other ear arrives through an extra relay that releases glycine and inhibits it. The louder side wins, so the cell's firing reports the level difference.

This nucleus gives most of its space to high frequencies, where level differences are large. The time comparator gives most of its space to low frequencies. Each nucleus favours the range where its cue works.
Both feed the inferior colliculus, where single cells first respond strongly to both cues. Losing one colliculus leaves an animal unable to locate sounds on the opposite side.

items: In headphones
A time cue pointing left and a level cue pointing right can cancel, and the sound seems straight ahead.
Balance
More of one cue moves the image to its side.
Where
Cells in the inferior colliculus respond to both cues together and are the likely basis.
In a room, reflections reach the ears from every wall, scrambling the time cue moment by moment.
Yet listeners point to the true source, because the first few milliseconds decide direction.
Delays up to about 0.6 ms pull the image toward the earlier speaker.
From about 0.6 to 10 ms, one sound is heard at the first speaker, but the room sounds fuller.
Beyond that, a distinct echo is heard.
blocks.end: Played backwards, a hammer striking a brick in a cathedral reveals a long swell of echoes we normally never notice.

entries.title: The Auditory Cortex
entries.what: The auditory cortex holds several frequency maps arranged in columns. It reorganises after hearing loss, is needed to locate sounds, and contains a region that responds to clear musical pitch.
entries.gives: It explains why the brain adapts to age-related hearing loss, and why pitch stays the same on a cheap speaker that cannot play the bass.
entries.pic: A strip of cortex with frequency bands in order and one enlarged band in bronze.

steps.t: Play a song through a tiny phone speaker, then through good headphones, at a comfortable volume.
The tune and the bass line keep the same pitch, though the small speaker produces almost no low frequencies.
Listen to the same note on two instruments, such as piano and guitar.
Same pitch, different quality. Pitch comes from the repeating pattern of the harmonics; quality from their balance.

entries.safety: Keep any test sound at a comfortable level, and stop at once if your ears ring or hurt.

words.meaning: Primary auditory cortex, the main frequency-mapped area of the hearing cortex.
A small ridge on the upper surface of the temporal lobe where A1 lies in humans.
Hearing the pitch of a note even when its lowest frequency is absent.
Hearing loss with age, mainly at high frequencies.

paras: The auditory cortex lies in the temporal lobe. In humans, primary cortex sits on Heschl's gyrus, hidden on the upper surface of the temporal lobe. Several fields each map frequency, and neighbouring maps meet in mirror image, as in vision.

A recording electrode going straight down through the six layers finds the same best frequency throughout: frequency is organised in columns. Many cortical cells also prefer a particular loudness and fall silent when the sound gets louder.

These maps were long thought fixed. Then experiments showed that after a small high-frequency hearing loss, the silent stretch of cortex takes up the neighbouring frequencies within weeks. The reorganisation grows larger at each stage up the pathway.

items: A small part of the cochlea is damaged, removing hearing at 10 to 20 kHz.
At first, the matching cortex simply falls silent.
After about three weeks, it responds to the edge frequencies instead.
Possible causes: new axon growth, or weak existing inputs being strengthened.
The same is likely in age-related hearing loss, which develops over decades.
blocks.end: Whether the enlarged areas improve hearing at those frequencies is still open.

items: One side lost
Removing A1 on one side leaves an animal unable to locate sounds on the opposite side.
Band by band
Removing only part of the map impairs localisation only for the matching frequencies.
Several fields
Reversible cooling shows A1 and two neighbouring fields are needed; others are not.
blocks.end: Each field likely does many things. Localisation is simply one that is well tested.

Invariance
Pitch stays the same across instruments, loudness and direction.
Missing fundamental
Remove the lowest component and the pitch stays, because the pattern still repeats at the same rate.
A pitch region
Brain scans show an area beside Heschl's gyrus active for clear pitch and quiet for weak pitch.
Lower stations
The brainstem and midbrain respond equally to strong and weak pitch.
Implants
Electrodes are ranked by pitch when an implant is first set up.

entries.title: Speech, Language and Bat Sonar
entries.what: Bats locate prey with echoes, and their cortex has cells tuned to the delay and pitch shift between call and echo. In humans, speech is decoded by a left-hemisphere network around the Sylvian fissure.
entries.gives: Comparing the two shows how a cortex specialises for the sounds that matter most to its owner, and explains common language disorders after stroke.
entries.pic: A bat sending a call to an insect, with the returning echo in bronze.

steps.t: Say "da" and "ga" slowly, feeling your tongue.
The difference lies in a fast frequency sweep at the start. Listeners hear one or the other, never a blend.
Say "ahhh" and hold it, then say "father".
Vowels can be held; stop consonants like "f" and "t" begin with a brief silence and a burst.
Watch bats over a lake at dusk, if they live near you.
They hunt in open air, where a single insect gives a single echo.

source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare · 9.04 Sensory Systems · Auditory cortex 2: language, bats and echolocation

words.meaning: Finding objects by sending out sounds and analysing their echoes.
A rise in pitch from a source moving closer, and a fall as it moves away.
A peak in the speech spectrum created by the shape of the vocal tract.
A disorder of understanding or producing language after brain damage.

paras: Echolocating bats send out calls far above human hearing and listen for echoes. The delay between call and echo gives distance. Near a target they call faster and faster, then fall silent while they eat.

Some tropical bats use a long constant tone. An echo from something moving returns slightly higher or lower in pitch, the Doppler shift, so they can pick out a fluttering moth among motionless leaves.
In their cortex, cells ignore a call or an echo alone and fire strongly to a call followed by an echo at one particular delay. Those delays are laid out in a map that corresponds to target distance.

items: Sweeping bats
Calls sweep from high to low pitch. They hunt in open air, over lakes and fields.
Steady-tone bats
Long constant tones end in a short sweep. They hunt in dense forest and detect movement by Doppler shift.
Fine detection
In early tests in darkness, bats avoided wires as thin as a human hair.
Delay tuning
Cells fire for call and echo separated by one delay, such as 9 ms.
Distance map
Delays of 0.4 to 18 ms are mapped in order, matching targets 7 to 310 cm away.
Acoustic fovea
A large part of the main map is given to 61 to 66 kHz, the pitch of the loudest call and its echoes.
Doppler area
Another region compares the steady tone of the call with that of the echo.
Synthesised calls
Researchers built artificial calls and echoes to find exactly which parts drive each cell.
Lower roots
Some delay tuning already appears in the inferior colliculus.
The vocal folds open and close, producing a buzz rich in harmonics.
The tongue, jaw and lips shape the vocal tract into a filter with peaks called formants.
Each vowel has its own formant pattern, held steady over time.
Consonants add silences, noise bursts and fast formant sweeps.
A small change in one sweep switches "da" to "ga" abruptly, with nothing heard in between.
blocks.end: Hearing continuous changes as sharp categories is called categorical perception.

items: Broca's area
Damage gives slow, effortful speech with missing small words. Comprehension is better.
Wernicke's area
Damage gives fluent speech but poor understanding.
A network
Scans show both areas, and the cortex around them, active even when people only listen.
blocks.end: In most right-handers language sits in the left hemisphere. Left-handers vary.

items: Stroke
Aphasia follows cortical damage; damage to the brainstem or thalamus rarely causes it.
One-sided anaesthesia
Before epilepsy surgery, putting one hemisphere briefly to sleep shows which side holds language.
Scans
A story in a known language lights up the left language network. An unknown language barely does.

blocks.text: Bats were long thought to avoid obstacles by touch. A student with an ultrasound detector first heard their calls in 1938, and named the ability echolocation.

entries.title: The NLP Communication Model
entries.what: NLP is a set of simple tools for changing how you think, feel and act.
entries.gives: You can change a reaction step by step, instead of only talking about it.
entries.pic: A funnel: lots of information goes into your mind, only a little gets through.

steps.t: Notice that your mind cannot take in everything around you.
It keeps a little, leaves a lot out, and fills the gaps with guesses.
So the world in your head is your own picture of it, not the world itself.
Listen to the words you use. They show your picture.
Choose one reaction you want to change.
Change one small thing, and see if the reaction changes.
